summary: Survey, design and adversarially verify ways to reuse representations while resolving conflicts locally

mtrl.summary:
Literature sweep on how multi-task deep RL and multi-task robot policy learning handle conflicts between tasks. Every paper listed was opened; entries marked 'abstract only' were checked against their arXiv or venue abstract alone.

(1) Gradient-level methods. PCGrad, CAGrad, Nash-MTL, FAMO, FairGrad and ConicGrad report Meta-World MT10 success rising from about 0.49 (multi-task SAC) to 0.72–0.91, against 0.90 for one SAC per task. These papers mostly copy one baseline table (Meta-World V1, best success over training, MTRL codebase). Re-evaluations undercut the gains:
- Kurin et al. 2022: a regularised plain sum of task losses matches every gradient method on MT10 and MT50.
- Meta-World+ 2025: PCGrad's published results do not reproduce (MT10 70.5 vs published 90; MT50 45.8 vs 70). Switching the reward version flips results (PaCo on MT10: 26.2 under V1, 73.6 under V2).
- MTBench 2025 (massively parallel PPO in IsaacGym): conflicts appear in the critic, not the actor. PCGrad scores below plain multi-task PPO. A critic-free MT-GRPO scores 91.1 on MT10-rand and 74.5 on MT50-rand, nearly matching every multi-task method.
- Supervised critiques (Xin et al. 2022, Royer et al. 2023, Elich et al. 2023/24) and parameter-scaling results (McLean et al. 2025, BRC 2025) agree: tuning and capacity, especially of the critic, explain most of the reported gains. Elich et al. also find that gradient conflicts between samples of one task are as large as conflicts between tasks. The only rebuttal is theoretical: Hu et al. 2023 show that a weighted sum of losses cannot reach balanced Pareto points in under-parameterised linear models.

(2) Architecture-level methods.
- Soft routing that depends on the state: Soft Modularization, CARE.
- Task-level composition or orthogonal experts: PaCo, MOORE.
- Module weights recomputed at every timestep, aimed at conflict inside a task: CMTA.
- Per-parameter task masks scored by gradient agreement: HarmoDT, SoCo-DT.
- Copying the layers or neurons where gradients conflict: Recon (layers, supervised); GradPS (clones neurons whose gradients from different agents cancel, multi-agent RL); DTME-MTL (adds task tokens, supervised).
- Mixture-of-experts: SDP (one router per task), MoDE (routing by noise level), MoE-Loco, and ScaleZero (proves a lower conflict bound than a dense layer and adds LoRA adapters as tasks are solved).
- Isolation and growth: CORAL (one LoRA per task on a VLA); CompoNet and SDP (new modules over frozen old ones).

(3) State-level localisation is rare.
- Memory Anchors: detects conflict states in the old policy's latent space, but the setting is continual imitation and the fix is replay.
- Gradient Coupling: similar states with good and bad actions interfere; its fix is a global auxiliary classifier, not localised.
- CMTA: routes per timestep but never detects conflict.
- QMP and CTPG: choose another task's behaviour per state for exploration, only in off-policy SAC.

(4) Recent robot and VLA RL work shows little interference once the policy starts from SFT. RLinf-VLA trains one model on 130 LIBERO tasks to 98.11%. πRL lifts π0.5 from 40.1% to 90.9% across 4,352 ManiSkill pick-and-place combinations. LLM studies report that RL updates are sparse and nearly orthogonal across tasks, and forget less than SFT. Under sparse reward or from scratch, the working fixes are task reweighting, demonstrations and behaviour sharing, not representation surgery. DGPO, for example, raises multi-task PPO from 42.5% to 85.2% on 40 state-based LIBERO tasks.

Verdict on our sketch:
- Each component exists separately: state-level conflict detection (Memory Anchors, Gradient Coupling), copying units where conflict is found (Recon, GradPS, DTME, HarmoDT), and per-state behaviour sharing for exploration (QMP, CTPG).
- The combination appears unclaimed: detect conflict states in the actor's latent space during on-policy, sparse-reward RL, copy only the units used there behind a task gate, and raise exploration noise there.
- The premise is weak where we would test it. In multi-task PPO the literature puts the bottleneck in the critic and in capacity. In cold start there is nothing to localise before the first success.
- Run the cheap critic-versus-actor-versus-capacity diagnosis described in open_gaps before building the method.

works.title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning (PCGrad)
works.setting: Supervised MTL; Meta-World MT10/MT50 with SAC
works.mechanism: Level: gradient. State-localised: no. If two task gradients conflict (g_i·g_j < 0), g_i is projected onto the normal plane of g_j (tasks taken in random order) and the modified gradients are summed. Conflict is measured per iteration over whole-task batches.
works.note: Reports that SAC+PCGrad solves all MT10 tasks and about 70% of MT50. In its own two-task analysis (reach vs press-button), conflicts are frequent while task 2 is unsolved and drop once task 2 is learned, i.e. conflict is a pre-mastery phenomenon. Meta-World+ could not reproduce: 70.5 (MT10) and 45.8 (MT50) on V1, vs published 90 and 70. MTBench with PPO: 86.21 vs plain 87.51 (MT10-rand); 59.74 vs 63.26 (MT50-rand).

works.title: Gradient Vaccine: Investigating and Improving Multi-task Optimization in Massively Multilingual Models (GradVac)
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 2010.05874 (ICLR 2021 from memory; the arXiv page lists no venue)
works.setting: Multilingual NMT and XTREME; no RL
works.mechanism: Level: gradient. State-localised: no. Pushes pairwise task-gradient similarity toward targets tracked along the training trajectory, encouraging more aligned updates for closely related tasks.
works.note: Abstract only. No RL results, so it says nothing about Meta-World.

works.title: Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent for Multi-task Learning (CAGrad)
works.setting: Supervised MTL; Meta-World MT10/MT50, SAC, MTRL codebase (CARE setup)
works.mechanism: Level: gradient. State-localised: no. Solves max_d min_i <g_i, d> subject to ||d - g0|| <= c||g0||: the update stays near the average gradient while maximising the worst task's local improvement.
works.note:
Table 3 (MT10 / MT50; 10 seeds; highest test success over 2M steps):
- MT-SAC 0.49 / 0.36
- MT-SAC + task encoder 0.54 / 0.40
- Multi-head SAC 0.61 / 0.45
- PCGrad 0.72 / 0.50
- Soft Modularization 0.73 / 0.50
- CAGrad 0.83 / 0.52
- CARE 0.84 / 0.54
- One SAC per task 0.90 / 0.74
Under MTBench PPO: 82.98 (below plain 87.51) on MT10-rand; 67.70 (above 63.26) on MT50-rand.

works.title: Multi-Task Learning as a Bargaining Game (Nash-MTL)
works.mechanism: Level: gradient. State-localised: no. The joint update direction is the Nash bargaining solution among task gradients.
works.note: Claims MT10 0.91 ± 0.03. FAMO's authors could not reproduce it: 0.80 ± 0.13 (update every step), 0.76 (every 50), 0.80 (every 100). The large standard errors signal instability.

works.title: FAMO: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization
works.setting: Supervised MTL; Meta-World MT10 (SAC, CAGrad setup)
works.mechanism: Level: loss weighting (gradient magnitude). State-localised: no. Dynamic task weights that make task losses decrease in a balanced way, at O(1) space and time.
works.note:
MT10: FAMO 0.83 ± 0.05; CAGrad 0.83; PCGrad 0.72; plain sum 0.49; per-task SAC 0.90.
MTBench PPO: 87.26 (MT10-rand) and 74.52 (MT50-rand), the best gradient-level method there. Since it only balances magnitudes, its success fits the view that magnitude imbalance, not angular conflict, matters.

works.title: Fair Resource Allocation in Multi-Task Learning (FairGrad)
works.setting: Supervised MTL; Meta-World MT10 (SAC, MTRL codebase, 2M steps)
works.mechanism: Level: gradient (alpha-fair utility over task improvements). State-localised: no.
works.note: MT10 0.84 ± 0.07, against the same copied rows (PCGrad 0.72, CAGrad 0.83, FAMO 0.83). The paper adopts FAMO's reproduced Nash-MTL value (0.80).

works.title: Fantastic Multi-Task Gradient Updates and How to Find Them In a Cone (ConicGrad)
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 2502.00217 (no venue stated in the PDF)
works.mechanism: Level: gradient (update constrained to a cone around the average gradient). State-localised: no.
works.note: MT10 0.89 ± 0.02 vs per-task SAC 0.90. It reuses the same copied baseline table and notes that Nash-MTL could not be reproduced.

works.title: Scalable Multi-Objective Robot Reinforcement Learning through Gradient Conflict Resolution (GCR-PPO)
works.setting: IsaacLab manipulation and locomotion; PPO; conflict between reward terms (task vs regularisers), not between tasks
works.mechanism: Level: gradient. State-localised: no. A multi-head critic gives per-objective actor gradients; conflicts are resolved by objective priority.
works.note: Abstract only. Average +9.5% over large-scale PPO, larger gains on high-conflict tasks. Shows that conflict handling inside PPO can help when the conflict is between reward terms.

works.title: In Defense of the Unitary Scalarization for Deep Multi-Task Learning
works.setting: Supervised MTL plus Meta-World MT10/MT50 (V1, SAC, fully shared 3x400 MLP)
works.mechanism: Level: critique. With a larger replay buffer, L2 on the actor and fixed reward normalisation, the plain sum of task losses matches PCGrad, MGDA, GradDrop, RLW and IMTL.
works.note:
'None of the SMTOs significantly outperforms' the plain sum on MT10/MT50; PCGrad is slightly above on MT50 with overlapping CIs.
- Runtime: one plain-sum run takes about 15 h; PCGrad, MGDA and GradDrop take more than a week.
- The authors suggest many of these optimisers act as regularisers, and that PopArt would mimic PCGrad's loss rescaling.

works.title: Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help?
works.setting: Supervised language (multilingual MT) and vision; no RL
works.mechanism: Level: critique. Large-scale study: specialised multi-task optimisers do not improve the interference profile beyond static loss weighting.
works.note: Reported gains often vanish with tuned learning rate and weight decay; some results did not reproduce.

works.title: Revisiting Scalarization in Multi-Task Learning: A Theoretical Perspective
works.setting: Linear MTL theory plus one real dataset
works.mechanism: Level: theory (rebuttal). In under-parameterised linear models, a weighted sum of losses cannot trace the full Pareto front, especially balanced trade-offs; specialised optimisers can reach balanced points it cannot.
works.note: The only rebuttal found, and it applies to the under-parameterised regime. That is exactly the regime where 'just make the network wider' is the competing fix.

works.title: Scalarization for Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Learning at Scale
works.setting: Supervised vision, multi-task and multi-domain, several model sizes
works.mechanism: Level: critique and loss weighting. A uniform weighted sum is on par with costly specialised optimisers; population-based training is proposed to search weights when there are many tasks.
works.note: Abstract only.

works.title: Examining Common Paradigms in Multi-Task Learning
works.mechanism: Level: analysis. Compares gradient conflict between tasks with conflict between samples of the same task.
works.overlaps_component: Critique of the premise for (1): conflict localisation needs a within-task null
works.note:
Key findings:
- 'No consistent evidence for gradient alignment conflicts ... to be an exclusive problem of having multiple tasks.'
- Conflicts 'can actually be even more pronounced between samples.'
- The MTL vs single-task difference is mainly gradient magnitude; Adam is a strong baseline.
Implication: latent neighbours with opposite advantage will also appear within one task.

works.title: Meta-World+: An Improved, Standardized, RL Benchmark
works.setting: Meta-World MT10/MT50/ML10/ML45, V1 vs V2 rewards
works.mechanism: Level: benchmark audit. Re-runs MTRL methods under both reward versions.
works.note:
Findings:
- 'We cannot replicate the published results from PCGrad.'
- All algorithms score higher with V2 rewards.
- MT10 V2: MT-MH-SAC 77.3, Soft-Mod 84.9, MOORE 83.4, PaCo 72.3, PCGrad 85.5.
- MT10 V1: PaCo 26.2, MT-MH-SAC 46.9.
- MT50 V2: MOORE 72.0, PCGrad 69.5, MT-MH-SAC 54.9.

works.title: Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning Enables Parameter Scaling
works.mechanism: Level: capacity. Scaling a simple multi-head SAC baseline to the parameter count of specialised architectures (Soft-Mod, PaCo, MOORE) outperforms them; most of the gain comes from scaling the critic.
works.overlaps_component: Evidence against (a); matched-capacity baseline needed for (2)
works.note:
Other findings:
- Reduced-critic configurations 'show substantial performance degradation.'
- More tasks reduce dormant neurons (plasticity loss).
Any 'grow/split units' method adds capacity, so it must beat a width-matched baseline.

works.title: Bigger, Regularized, Categorical: High-Capacity Value Functions are Efficient Multi-Task Learners (BRC)
works.setting: 7 multi-task benchmarks, more than 280 tasks (incl. Meta-World 50, HumanoidBench); value-based actor-critic
works.mechanism: Level: capacity plus loss (critic). Large normalised residual Q-networks with a cross-entropy (categorical) loss and learnable task embeddings.
works.note: 'Increasing the parameter count reduces the rate of gradient conflicts' (measured on HumanoidBench-Medium). Gradient surgery 'might not be required after a certain model scale.' Beats PCGrad, PaCo and CTPG on Meta-World (numbers in figures only).

works.title: Benchmarking Massively Parallelized Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning for Robotics Tasks (MTBench)
works.setting: IsaacGym: 50 Meta-World tasks plus 20 Parkour tasks; MT-PPO, MT-GRPO, MT-SAC, MT-PQN; 1B frames, 10 seeds
works.mechanism: Level: benchmark and analysis. Gradient methods (PCGrad, CAGrad, FAMO) and architectures (Soft-Mod, CARE, PaCo, MOORE) on top of massively parallel PPO, plus an analysis of actor vs critic task-gradient cosine.
works.overlaps_component: Closest testbed to ours (GPU-sim PPO); direct evidence against actor-side premise for (a)
works.note:
Success, MT10-rand / MT50-rand:
- Plain MT-PPO 87.5 / 63.3
- PCGrad 86.2 / 59.7
- CAGrad 83.0 / 67.7
- FAMO 87.3 / 74.5
- Multi-head MOORE 86.9 / 79.5
- PaCo 84.4 / 70.5
- Critic-free MT-GRPO 91.1 / 74.5
Conflicts arise 'when learning the critic network in MT-PPO' but 'we do not observe similar conflicts in policy optimization'; conclusion: 'Value learning is the key bottleneck in MTRL.' Gradient methods give only marginal gains on sparse Parkour. MT-PPO here uses per-task value and input normalisation.

works.title: TOPPO: Rethinking PPO for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Critic Balancing
works.mechanism: Level: critic (gradient conditioning). Critic-balancing modules fix 'critic-side gradient ill-conditioning', where easy tasks dominate value updates and tail tasks stall.
works.note: Abstract only. Reports better mean and tail-task results than SAC-family and ARS-family baselines, with fewer parameters and environment steps; no numbers on the page.

works.title: Proactive Gradient Conflict Mitigation in Multi-Task Learning: A Sparse Training Perspective
works.mechanism: Level: parameters. Update only a subset of parameters to reduce how often conflicts occur.
works.note: Abstract only. Claims gradient manipulation 'cannot decrease the incidence of gradient conflict', the same claim as Recon.

works.title: Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Soft Modularization
works.mechanism: Level: representation (soft routing). State-localised: implicitly. A routing network takes the task embedding and the current state and outputs per-layer soft probabilities over modules; the loss is weighted per task via SAC temperatures.
works.note: Routing depends on state but has no explicit conflict detection. CAGrad table: 0.73 (MT10) / 0.50 (MT50). MTBench PPO: 82.96 / 67.72. In CMTA's reproduction without the loss-weighting trick: 51% (MT10-Fixed).

works.title: Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Context-based Representations (CARE)
works.mechanism: Level: representation. State-localised: implicitly. Mixture of k state encoders with attention alpha_j = softmax(z_enc^j(s) · z_context), where z_context comes from a frozen language model encoding the task description.
works.note: CAGrad table: 0.84 (MT10) / 0.54 (MT50), using extra metadata. MTBench multi-head CARE with PPO: 84.79 / 71.05.

works.title: PaCo: Parameter-Compositional Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning
works.mechanism: Level: parameters. State-localised: no. Task parameters theta_tau = Phi w_tau, a task-specific mix of a shared parameter set. For tasks whose loss explodes: mask that task's loss and re-initialise only its w ('w-reset').
works.overlaps_component: (2) task-specific parameters; isolation of failing tasks
works.note: Results are very sensitive to reward version: Meta-World+ reproduction 26.2 (V1) vs 73.6 (V2) on MT10. MTBench PPO: 84.37 / 70.46.

works.title: Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE)
works.mechanism: Level: representation. State-localised: no (expert weights come from a task encoder on a one-hot id). k experts encode the state; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalises their representations; task weights combine them; used in both actor and critic.
works.note: Reports 88.7 ± 5.6 (MT10-rand) and 72.9 ± 3.3 (MT50-rand). Meta-World+ reproduces 83.2 / 72.0 (V2) and 61.4 / 61.2 (V1). Best MT50 method in MTBench PPO (multi-head MOORE 79.46).

works.title: Contrastive Modules with Temporal Attention for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (CMTA)
works.setting: Meta-World MT10/MT50 (Fixed and Mixed), SAC, 8 seeds
works.mechanism: Level: representation. State-localised: per timestep. Six expert encoders; weights from an LSTM state history plus a task embedding, recomputed every step. An InfoNCE loss makes experts differ (positive = the same expert at t+1). Targets 'negative transfer within a task' (e.g. the reach vs push phases of Push).
works.note:
No explicit conflict detection and no direct measurement of within-task conflict. Max-smoothed success:
- MT10-Fixed: CMTA 78.95 vs CARE 68.03 vs single-task SAC 64.33
- MT50-Mixed: CMTA 71.69
Best success over training on probably V1, so the numbers are not comparable across papers.

works.title: HarmoDT: Harmony Multi-Task Decision Transformer for Offline Reinforcement Learning
works.setting: Offline MTRL, Meta-World (up to 50 tasks), Decision Transformer
works.mechanism: Level: parameters. State-localised: no (task-level). Bi-level meta-learning of a binary mask per task. Per-parameter agreement score = elementwise task gradient × mean gradient, plus magnitude or Fisher importance. Periodically masks the most conflicting, least important weights and recovers those that turned harmonious, at fixed sparsity.
works.note: Per-parameter conflict localisation, but per task and offline; it masks rather than grows.

works.title: Soft Conflict-Resolution Decision Transformer for Offline Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (SoCo-DT)
works.mechanism: Level: parameters. State-localised: no. Soft masks: Fisher importance keeps key parameters, conflict scores suppress conflicting ones; per-task thresholds from an IQR rule on conflict/harmony score distributions with cosine-annealed updates.
works.note: Abstract only. +7.6% over the previous best on MT50; +10.5% on suboptimal data.

works.title: Recon: Reducing Conflicting Gradients from the Root for Multi-Task Learning
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (architecture). State-localised: no. Scores each shared layer by how often its task gradients conflict, makes the top-scoring layers task-specific, then retrains with any optimiser.
works.note: Abstract only. Claims gradient surgery 'cannot effectively reduce the occurrence of conflicting gradients'. Only a small parameter increase in many cases.

works.title: GradPS: Resolving Futile Neurons in Parameter Sharing Network for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
works.setting: Cooperative MARL with parameter sharing (SMAC); agents play the role of tasks
works.mechanism:
Level: parameters (neuron cloning). State-localised: no (groups agents, not states).
- Neuron gradient conflict C_ij = sum_T (|phi_i| + |phi_j| - |phi_i + phi_j|) at the activation, accumulated over a target-update interval.
- 'Futile neurons' have gradient efficiency below 0.2.
- Each futile neuron gets K clones, each shared by a group of agents whose gradients conflict little.
works.overlaps_component: (2) split only the few units where gradients cancel, with group-gated copies
works.note: Essentially our component (2) already done, with agents in place of tasks and no state localisation. Reviewers will cite it.

works.title: Resolving Token-Space Gradient Conflicts: Token Space Manipulation for Transformer-Based Multi-Task Learning (DTME-MTL)
works.setting: Supervised dense-prediction MTL with pretrained transformers
works.mechanism: Level: representation (tokens). State-localised: no. Detects conflicts in token space and responds by type: affine modulation of existing tokens, or adding new task-specific tokens (expansion).
works.note: Abstract only on arXiv; the range-space vs null-space split comes from secondary summaries and was not checked. Claims parameter-duplication methods such as Recon overfit on transformers.

works.title: One Model for All Tasks: Leveraging Efficient World Models in Multi-Task Planning (ScaleZero)
works.setting: Online multi-task model-based RL (UniZero), Atari26, DMC18, Jericho
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (MoE plus growth). State-localised: through per-input gating. MoE feed-forward layers replace dense ones; Theorem 5.1 gives a strictly lower gradient-conflict upper bound than dense layers. Dynamic Parameter Scaling adds a LoRA adapter per stage (old ones frozen), triggered by task progress or a budget, not by conflict.
works.note: Atari26 mean human-normalised score: ScaleZero (multi-task) 0.39 vs single-task UniZero 0.38 vs dense multi-task 0.31. DPS reaches the target with 71.5% of the environment interactions on DMC.

works.title: Mixture-of-Experts Meets In-Context Reinforcement Learning (T2MIR)
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (MoE). Token-wise MoE (state/action/reward tokens) in parallel with task-wise MoE; the task router is trained contrastively (InfoNCE) to reduce gradient conflict across a heterogeneous task distribution.
works.note: Abstract only.

works.title: Sparse Diffusion Policy: A Sparse, Reusable, and Flexible Policy for Robot Learning (SDP)
works.setting: Multi-task imitation (MimicGen 8 tasks, DexArt, Adroit, real FANUC); continual learning (robomimic)
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (sparse MoE in a diffusion transformer). State-localised: no (one router per task, top-2 of 8 experts). In continual learning, old experts and routers are frozen and new experts plus a new router are added.
works.overlaps_component: (2) grow new units over frozen old ones; (b) router-only transfer
works.note: MimicGen average: 0.76 vs 0.73 for the best dense baseline. Routing alone transfers to Coffee Preparation at 0.80 with about 0.1M trainable parameters, vs 0.70 from scratch. Interference is not measured.

works.title: Efficient Diffusion Transformer Policies with Mixture of Expert Denoisers for Multitask Learning (MoDE)
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (sparse MoE). Routing is conditioned on the diffusion noise level, not on the task, so it is a compute-efficiency device rather than conflict resolution.
works.note: LIBERO-90 0.95, CALVIN ABC 4.01 with pretraining.

works.title: MoE-Loco: Mixture of Experts for Multitask Locomotion
works.setting: PPO in IsaacGym (4096 envs), quadruped and biped gaits across terrains
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (MoE in actor and critic). State-localised: implicitly (gate on an LSTM state over latent state and command).
works.note:
Gradient-conflict measurements (MoE vs MLP):
- Bar vs Stair cosine: 0.278 vs -0.132
- Bar vs Stair negative-entry share: 45.5% vs 55.1%
- Mixed-task success: 0.879 vs 0.571
The dense MLP is not width-matched as far as reported.

works.title: CORAL: Scalable Multi-Task Robot Learning via LoRA Experts
works.setting: Multi-task VLA fine-tuning (SFT): LIBERO, WidowX, Google Robot, real Galaxea R1
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (strict isolation). State-localised: no. Frozen VLA backbone plus one LoRA per task, selected by instruction.
works.note: Abstract only. Motivated by gradient conflicts in joint fine-tuning; 'substantially outperforms joint training' (no numbers on the abstract page). SFT, not RL.

works.title: Self-Composing Policies for Scalable Continual Reinforcement Learning (CompoNet)
works.mechanism: Level: parameters (growth). Adds one module per task that can selectively combine earlier policies with its own; parameters grow linearly with the number of tasks.
works.overlaps_component: (b) grow new impressions on top of old policies
works.note: Abstract only. Grows a whole module per task, with no conflict localisation.

works.title: QMP: Q-switch Mixture of Policies for Multi-Task Behavior Sharing
works.setting: Off-policy MTRL (SAC): Meta-World MT10/MT50 and a CDS 4-task set, locomotion, navigation
works.mechanism: Level: data/behaviour. State-localised: yes. At every state of task i, each task policy proposes its mean action; the one with the highest Q_i collects the step. The learning objective is unchanged.
works.overlaps_component: (3) use other-task knowledge for exploration at specific states; similar to the WRWL gate
works.note: Shares less from conflicting tasks, and sharing falls as each policy improves. Adds gains on top of PCGrad in 3 of 4 environments. Not on-policy, and uses Q-values rather than representation conflict.

works.title: Efficient Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Cross-Task Policy Guidance (CTPG)
works.mechanism: Level: data/behaviour. State-localised: yes (every K = 10 steps). A guide policy picks which task's control policy acts for the next K steps. A filter gate keeps policy j only if guide Q(s, j) >= V_i(s); a block gate guides only harder tasks.
works.overlaps_component: (3) conflict-aware exploration via other tasks' behaviour
works.note:
Success, base → with CTPG:
- MT10 MTSAC 62.7 → 75.8
- MT50 Soft-Mod 55.0 → 66.2
- PaCo MT10 69.8 → 70.4 (+0.6 only)

works.title: Conservative Data Sharing for Multi-Task Offline Reinforcement Learning (CDS)
works.setting: Offline MTRL: locomotion, navigation, vision-based manipulation
works.mechanism: Level: data. State-localised: per transition. Routes other tasks' data into a task only where it improves on the task's own data (conservative Q criterion).
works.note: Abstract only. Naive sharing hurts because it worsens distribution shift.

works.title: Multi-task Deep Reinforcement Learning with PopArt
works.venue_or_id: AAAI 2019 (per Kurin et al.'s reference); arXiv 1809.04474
works.mechanism: Level: loss/output (adaptive per-task normalisation of value targets so tasks have similar influence on updates). State-localised: no.
works.overlaps_component: Baseline that must be in any (a) pilot
works.note: Kurin et al. argue PopArt-style rescaling explains part of PCGrad's RL gains. Our backup topic 'Aliased, Not Overloaded' already assumes a LayerNorm critic plus per-task PopArt.

works.title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
works.setting: Continual imitation (diffusion policy, π0.5) on LIBERO plus 2 real tasks, experience replay
works.mechanism:
Level: data (replay selection). State-localised: yes.
- Find new-task samples whose embedding under the old policy falls inside old-task data (kNN distance stats plus 2-means).
- Among those, keep samples where the old policy's noise-and-denoise action disagrees with the label (above mu + 2 sigma).
- Replay the old samples nearest to these conflict points.
works.overlaps_component: (1) locate conflict in representation space (old policy's latent plus action disagreement)
works.note:
Results: excluding 10% of anchors raises forgetting more than 4.5x; anchors cut forgetting on high-conflict task pairs by 63%.
It relies on new-task action labels (demonstrations). Sparse-reward RL cold start has none, which is the gap for setting (b).

works.title: Gradient Coupling: The Hidden Barrier to Generalization in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
works.setting: Single-task agentic LLM RL (GRPO), ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, Qwen2.5-3B/7B
works.mechanism: Level: representation (auxiliary loss). State-localised: no. Similar but distinct states make gradient updates interfere (reinforcing a good action in one raises a bad one in another). An auxiliary objective trains the actor to also classify actions as good or bad, separating their embeddings. Labels are heuristic (repeated observation = bad, final step = good) or from DeepSeek-V3, not advantage-based; the loss is applied globally.
works.overlaps_component: (1) plus representation separation, i.e. our backup 'Aliased, Not Overloaded'
works.note: ALFWorld out-of-domain (Qwen-7B): GRPO 48.1 → 57.2. A localised, advantage-labelled version restricted to coupled states remains open, but the core idea is published.

open_gaps: No paper found that combines all three parts of the sketch in online RL: detect conflict at the state level in the actor's latent space, add parameters only for those states (state-gated copies of units), and train on-policy with sparse rewards. The closest pieces each cover one part: Memory Anchors detects conflict states but in continual imitation, and fixes it with replay. GradPS clones conflicting neurons, but groups by agent and is value-based multi-agent RL. CMTA weights modules per timestep but never detects conflict. Gradient Coupling adds a global auxiliary loss, not a localised one. HarmoDT and SoCo-DT learn per-parameter masks per task, offline.

Nobody uses representation conflict as an exploration signal in on-policy multi-task RL. QMP and CTPG pick another task's behaviour at specific states, but only for data collection in off-policy SAC. Raising exploration noise in a state-dependent way at conflict states, which our 'no resets' rule allows, is untested. Our StackCube logs suggest that gripper noise, not anchoring, decides success.

No published work splits a from-scratch, sparse-binary-reward, GPU-sim multi-task PPO collapse like the lab's (97.9% single-task to about 32–36% with ten tasks) into causes: critic, actor, task imbalance, capacity, or noise. MTBench did this only on dense-reward Meta-World, and found the critic to blame.

Hypothesis (my inference, not from the literature): with sparse rewards, much of the 'interference' may be noise rather than conflict. Unsolved tasks produce no signal, so per-batch advantage normalisation turns critic noise into full-size actor updates that erode shared skills. The full-finetune drift of 2.5 nats in the first update on StackCube fits this. A gate that drops a task from the actor loss until its returns vary (as GRPO drops all-fail groups) is the trivial competitor.

Cold start (setting b): no method resolves conflict before the new task's first success, because there is no new-task signal to locate. Memory Anchors works only because it has demonstrations. Any version of the sketch must either use a proxy (WRWL's source-side proxies scored 0/5 against simple heuristics) or wait for first successes. The latter turns into WRWL's A3 fallback, whose lead over CUP and QMP is only marginal.

Sparse-reward evidence is thin. Almost all multi-task results are dense-reward Meta-World under a best-over-training metric with copied baselines; the one sparse case (MTBench Parkour) shows only marginal gains from gradient methods.

Any 'grow/split' result must be compared against matched-capacity baselines: a wider actor and critic (McLean), MoE (ScaleZero, MOORE) and a multi-head critic with per-task normalisation (PopArt). Any conflict detector also needs a within-task null (Elich et al.) and a label-shuffle control (lesson from WRWL G3').
evidence_against_premise: In massively parallel multi-task PPO, the closest setting to our testbed, conflict sits in the critic, not the actor. MTBench says conflicts arise 'when learning the critic network in MT-PPO' and 'we do not observe similar conflicts in policy optimization'. A critic-free MT-GRPO scores 91.1 (MT10-rand) and 74.5 (MT50-rand) against 87.5 and 63.3 for plain MT-PPO, nearly matching every multi-task method. TOPPO (2026) separately blames critic-side gradient ill-conditioning. Our sketch puts the conflict in the actor's representations.

Capacity explains much of what is called conflict. McLean et al. 2025 show a plain baseline scaled to matched parameters beats Soft-Mod, PaCo and MOORE, with most of the gain from scaling the critic. BRC 2025 reports that larger models have fewer gradient conflicts and that 'complex interventions such as gradient surgery might not be required after a certain model scale'. Our actor is a 3x256 Tanh MLP, so 'too small' is the simplest explanation of the ten-task drop.

Optimiser-level conflict resolution rarely beats a tuned plain sum of task losses:
- Kurin et al. 2022: none of the specialised optimisers significantly beats it on MT10/MT50, and PCGrad costs about 9 days per MT50 run vs 15 h.
- Xin et al. 2022 and Royer et al. 2023 find the same in supervised MTL.
- The MT10 table reused by CAGrad, FAMO, FairGrad and ConicGrad rests on copied baselines measured as best success over training on Meta-World V1.
- Meta-World+ could not reproduce PCGrad (70.5 / 45.8 vs published 90 / 70), and reward version alone moves PaCo's MT10 score from 26.2 to 73.6.

Angular gradient conflict is not specific to multiple tasks. Elich et al. find it 'can actually be even more pronounced between samples' of a single task; what separates multi-task from single-task training is gradient magnitude. So 'latent neighbours with opposite advantage' will be common within one task, from advantage noise, and a detector without a within-task null measures noise. WRWL's label-shuffle result (true labels no better than shuffled on StackCube) already showed this kind of failure.

Under sparse rewards and at cold start, gradient- and representation-level resolution has little to act on:
- MTBench: gradient methods give only 'relatively marginal' gains on sparse Parkour.
- Multi-task GRPO: all-fail groups contribute zero gradient.
- PCGrad's own analysis: conflicts are frequent only while a task is still unsolved.
- The fixes that work target imbalance and exploration (MT-GRPO reweighting; IW-PPO), demonstrations (DGPO raises MT-PPO from 42.5% to 85.2% on 40 LIBERO tasks and collapses to 5.1% without its BC term), or behaviour sharing (QMP, CTPG).
- Our own StackCube runs succeed or fail with exploration noise and seed, not with where the anchor sits.

For the eventual VLA target, interference is not a visible bottleneck in RL post-training. RLinf-VLA trains one OpenVLA-OFT on 130 LIBERO tasks with GRPO from 42.1% to 98.1%; πRL lifts π0.5 from 40.1% to 90.9% over 4,352 ManiSkill combinations. LLM studies find RL updates are sparse and nearly orthogonal across tasks ('SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists') and forget less than SFT because they stay KL-close (RL's Razor). Reports of conflict in VLAs (e.g. CORAL) concern SFT, not RL.

Each sub-mechanism of the sketch is already published:
- State-level conflict localisation in the old policy's latent space: Memory Anchors; similar-state interference fixed by embedding separation: Gradient Coupling.
- Duplicating units where gradients conflict: Recon (layers), GradPS (neurons, group-gated clones), DTME-MTL (tokens), HarmoDT and SoCo-DT (parameter masks).
- Growing new modules over frozen old ones: CompoNet, SDP, ScaleZero.
- Per-state cross-task behaviour selection for exploration: QMP, CTPG.
Novelty would rest only on the combination and the sparse-reward on-policy setting. Reviewers will ask why a matched-capacity MoE or a per-task critic is not enough.

Our own results argue against cold-start localisation (setting b). WRWL's source-side conflict predictors were 0/5 against simple heuristics, and value-based 'gold' labels marked as safe exactly the release region where new behaviour had to be learned. Before the first success, new-task advantages are critic noise, so 'opposite-advantage neighbours' cannot be told apart from noise.

growth.summary:
This was a read-only sweep: I edited no files and ran nothing. I read the local context in /home/ryan/Documents/pve/docs/morning-2026-10-31.md, final-topic-report.md §8, /home/ryan/Documents/pve/wrwl/ppo.py, wrwl/shared.py, wrwl/envs/unified.py and the Memory Anchors notes. In ppo.py the actor is a 3x256 tanh MLP with one state-independent log-std. SharedPolicy has a 2x256 trunk plus a head. I opened about 80 papers or pages.

VERDICT BY SKETCH COMPONENT

(1) Locating conflict in representation space is not new on its own.
- The same detector already exists in several forms: Memory Anchors (latent kNN plus action disagreement), OWL's 'same state, different task' interference (AAAI 2022), PSM contrastive behaviour embeddings, HarmoDT/SoCo-DT per-parameter gradient-agreement scores, and RECON/CoNAL gradient-cosine scores.
- Our own backup idea 'Aliased, Not Overloaded' already uses exactly this detector: actor-latent neighbours whose advantages point in opposite directions.

(2) 'Grow or split where tasks conflict' is crowded at task x layer, module or parameter granularity.
- 'PCGrad but with a structural mechanism' is literally RECON's pitch (ICLR 2023, supervised only). RECON's own controls that pick layers or parameters at random do not work.
- CoNAL (AAAI 2023) branches modules when it detects conflict and reports Meta-World MT10 with SAC.
- DEN duplicates units whose incoming weights drift, per task.
- HarmoDT and SoCo-DT learn per-task masks that account for conflict, in offline multi-task RL on Meta-World.
- NBSP protects 'RL skill neurons' by gradient masking.
- SSDE splits parameters into frozen forward-transfer and trainable task-specific sets in continual RL.
- Function-preserving growth tools already exist: plasticity injection (h_θ + h_θ1' − h_θ2'), GradMax, and splitting steepest descent (child units at θ±εv_min).
- Units or routing that are local to a state, rather than gated by task, also exist, but they are learned end to end or keyed by retrieval, not triggered by a detected conflict:
  - Soft Modularization routes on state x task embedding (Meta-World).
  - CMTA attends over modules per step.
  - SDP, IsCiL, PhaseLoRA and LoRA-SP route adapters per input, state or action chunk (all supervised imitation).
  - PEX picks between a frozen old policy and a new policy per state using Q.
- Tabular RL split state cells where value or policy disagrees decades ago: Munos & Moore 1999, Continuous U-Tree 1998, and Platt's resource-allocating network 1990.
- What I did NOT find:
  - conflict-triggered, state-gated, function-preserving duplication of hidden units inside an on-policy actor;
  - any RL study that compares a conflict-selected split with a randomly selected split at equal parameter count.
- That combination is the remaining gap. Its novelty would be incremental; my estimate is about 3-4/10.

(3) Using conflict as an exploration signal was not found as such. The nearest are QMP (shares behaviour across tasks per state via the current task's Q), ClonEx-SAC (uses old policies for exploration) and SSDE (resets dormant neurons to explore).

PREMISE CHECK

Setting (a), multi-task with one shared network: the evidence against is strong.
- Kurin 2022: on Meta-World MT10/MT50 with SAC, a properly stabilised plain sum of task losses matches PCGrad and the other gradient-surgery methods.
- McLean 2025: a simple baseline scaled to equal parameters beats Soft Modularization, PaCo and MOORE, and the gains come mostly from the critic, not the actor.
- BRC 2025: the rate of gradient conflicts falls as width grows.
- Elich 2024: conflicts in gradient direction are not specific to multi-task learning; differences in gradient magnitude are what set it apart.
- RLinf-VLA: one OpenVLA-OFT model trained with GRPO reaches 98.11% on 130 LIBERO tasks.
- 'Simple Recipe Works' (RLC 2026): with LoRA and on-policy RL, VLAs forget less than 2% under sequential RL. Forgetting appears only for a ~12M-parameter policy, without LoRA, or with SFT.

Setting (b), cold-start transfer: growth cannot create the missing signal.
- Before the first success, advantages are critic noise, so 'neighbours with opposite advantage' are undefined.
- The Stack failure we observed comes from exploration (the gripper noise either snowballs or collapses) and from critic noise eroding the reused skills.
- Known recipes that do not involve growth already target both: critic or value warm-up (VLA-RL, FORCE), LP-FT, a frozen or plasticity-injected trunk, PEX, and BC/kickstarting retention (Wołczyk 2024). Wołczyk 2022 found that the critic carries most of the forward transfer.

SUGGESTED ORDER BEFORE BUILDING THE METHOD
1. Re-measure the 97.9% to 32-36% drop against a strong baseline at equal parameter count: critic at least 1024 wide, PopArt per task, LayerNorm, and a learned task embedding.
2. Only if a gap remains, compare conflict-selected with random-selected unit duplication at equal parameter count.
3. For (b), first test a frozen or injected trunk plus value-only warm-up plus a state-dependent gripper std, before framing anything as 'growth'.

works.title: Recon: Reducing Conflicting Gradients from the Root for Multi-Task Learning
works.setting: supervised MTL (Multi-Fashion+MNIST, CelebA, CityScapes, NYUv2, PASCAL-Context); no RL
works.mechanism: S-conflict score per shared layer = number of task pairs with cos(g_i,g_j)<S, summed over iterations; top-K layers are duplicated into task-specific copies and the network retrained.
works.overlaps_component: C2 grow/split where conflicted (task-gated, layer-level); the 'PCGrad but structural' framing
works.note: Read from the PDF text. It turns 0.26-12.77% of the shared parameters task-specific, and the model grows by 0.5-57%. Random-layer and random-parameter controls (RSL/RSP) do not work. The conflict layers it finds are 'mostly determined by architecture' and stay consistent across datasets and training stages.

works.title: Learning Conflict-Noticed Architecture for Multi-Task Learning (CoNAL)
works.venue_or_id: AAAI 2023 (ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/26312; that page was bot-blocked, so I read the text mirror)
works.setting: CV MTL plus RL (Meta-World MT10, SAC)
works.mechanism: If the cosine between task gradients on a shared module is negative, that module and later shared modules get zero gradient, so tasks update their task-specific modules instead; each task learns a branch point through a softmax.
works.overlaps_component: C2 conflict-triggered structural split, task-gated, module-level, in RL
works.note: Closest RL prior for 'grow where conflicted'. On MT10, as read from the mirror: success 0.76 versus 0.78 for single-task policies, with a 6.25x training speedup. I did not check whether it includes a random-branch control.

works.title: Lifelong Learning with Dynamically Expandable Networks (DEN)
works.mechanism: Selective retraining, expansion, then split/duplication: a unit whose incoming weights drift by an L2 distance greater than σ after training on the new task is copied. Units are timestamped, so old tasks only use units that existed at their stage.
works.overlaps_component: C2 unit duplication from old units (task-gated); C4 protect old meaning
works.note: Drift is a proxy for conflict. The split is per task, not per state. No RL experiments.

works.title: Splitting Steepest Descent for Growing Neural Architectures
works.mechanism: Per-neuron splitting matrix S(θ)=E_x[Φ'(σ(θ,x))∇²σ(θ,x)]. If its smallest eigenvalue is negative, the neuron is split into two children θ±εv_min with weights 1/2, which leaves the function unchanged at the moment of the split.
works.overlaps_component: C2 unit-level split triggered by the data, growing new units from old ones
works.note: Definition read from the PDF. The expectation runs over the whole data distribution. Restricting it to conflict states would turn it into a local split; I found no paper that does this.

works.title: Firefly Neural Architecture Descent
works.mechanism: Grows wider and deeper by steepest descent over a functional neighbourhood (splitting existing neurons and adding new ones), with greedy selection from a Taylor approximation.
works.note: Applied to continual learning; not RL.

works.title: GradMax: Growing Neural Networks using Gradient Information
works.mechanism: Adds neurons without changing the learned function; the new weights are initialised (via SVD) to maximise the gradient norm.

works.title: Growing Tiny Networks: Spotting Expressivity Bottlenecks and Fixing Them Optimally
works.mechanism: Detects where the desired functional update cannot be expressed by the current parameters (an expressivity bottleneck) and adds neurons there.

works.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Plasticity Injection
works.mechanism: Freezes head θ and outputs h_θ(x)+h_θ1'(x)−h_θ2'(x) with θ1'=θ2' at injection, so predictions are unchanged. The encoder stays shared and trainable, and all heads send gradients into it. Used both as a diagnostic and to grow the network.
works.overlaps_component: C2 function-preserving growth of new impressions on top of old ones; C4 protect
works.note: Construction read from the PDF. It is global (not state-gated) and has no notion of conflict. It is the cleanest template for 'grow new from old without changing behaviour'.

works.title: The Dormant Neuron Phenomenon in Deep RL (ReDo)
works.mechanism: Detects inactive neurons and recycles them during training.

works.title: Neuroplastic Expansion in Deep Reinforcement Learning
works.mechanism: Grows the network from small toward full size by adding neurons where potential gradients are large, prunes dormant neurons, and consolidates through experience review.
works.overlaps_component: C2 network growth in RL (global, not conflict-based)

works.title: Growing with Experience: Growing Neural Networks in Deep RL (GrowNN)
works.mechanism: Adds layers during RL without changing the encoded function.
works.note: Reports up to +48% on MiniHack Room and +72% on Ant versus static networks of the same size.

works.title: Maintaining Plasticity in Deep Continual Learning (continual backprop)
works.mechanism: Reinitialises a small fraction of low-utility units after each example.

works.title: Progressive Neural Networks
works.mechanism: Adds a new column per task with lateral connections to the frozen features of previous columns.
works.overlaps_component: C4 protect reused representation; C2 grow per task
works.note: Growth is per task, and parameters grow linearly with the number of tasks.

works.title: Sim-to-Real Robot Learning from Pixels with Progressive Nets
works.setting: robot manipulation, deep RL, sparse rewards
works.mechanism: Progressive nets carry policies learned in simulation over to a real arm.

works.title: PackNet
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 1711.05769 (CVPR 2018 from memory; not on the page)
works.mechanism: Iterative pruning frees redundant weights for new tasks.
works.note: It was the best prior method on Continual World (80%) according to Wołczyk 2022.

works.title: Piggyback
works.mechanism: Learns a binary mask per task over a frozen backbone.

works.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting with hard attention to the task (HAT)
works.mechanism: Learns a hard attention mask per task; earlier tasks' masks condition the new task's learning.

works.title: Gradient Projection Memory (GPM)
works.mechanism: Runs SVD on activations to find a core gradient subspace per task, then steps new tasks orthogonally to the stored subspaces.
works.note: Two searches found no RL evaluation.

works.title: Adam-NSCL: Training Networks in Null Space of Feature Covariance
works.mechanism: Projects Adam updates into the approximate null space of earlier tasks' uncentred input-feature covariance, per layer.

works.title: TRGP: Trust Region Gradient Projection
works.mechanism: Per layer, picks correlated old tasks using the norm of the gradient projected onto their input subspace, reuses their frozen weights through a scaling matrix, and updates orthogonally to them.

works.title: CUBER: Continual Learning with Backward Knowledge Transfer
works.mechanism: Uses gradient projection to find positively correlated old tasks layer by layer and lets updates modify their models.

works.title: InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning
works.mechanism: Designs the LoRA subspace so that tuning it causes no interference with old tasks.

works.title: Learning to Branch for Multi-Task Learning
works.mechanism: Learns tree-structured branching end to end, treating each branching decision as a Gumbel-softmax sample.

works.title: Branched Multi-Task Networks: Deciding What Layers To Share
works.mechanism: Builds a branched network under a parameter budget from task affinities.

works.title: Efficiently Identifying Task Groupings (TAG)
works.mechanism: Measures lookahead inter-task affinity (how one task's gradient step changes another task's loss) and groups tasks by it.

works.title: Multi-Task RL with Soft Modularization
works.mechanism: The routing network takes state features x task embedding (an elementwise product f(s)·h(z)) and outputs soft weights over modules for each sample.
works.note: Routing equations read from the PDF. Routing is learned end to end and is not triggered by conflict.

works.title: Contrastive Modules with Temporal Attention for MTRL (CMTA)
works.mechanism: Combines shared modules at a finer granularity than tasks, using temporal attention per step; a contrastive loss keeps modules diverse.

works.title: Dynamic Depth Routing for MTRL (D2R)
works.mechanism: Learns to skip modules so tasks use different depths.

works.title: MOORE: MTRL with Mixture of Orthogonal Experts
works.mechanism: Orthogonalises expert representations with Gram-Schmidt and combines them per task.

works.title: PaCo: Parameter-Compositional MTRL
works.mechanism: Learns a shared parameter set; each task's policy is an interpolation within that subspace.

works.title: HarmoDT: Harmony Multi-Task Decision Transformer
works.mechanism: Learns a binary per-parameter mask per task by bi-level meta-learning. The harmony score is gradient agreement (g_i ⊙ mean g) plus λ·importance (|θ| or Fisher); sparsity is 0.2 and masked weights are re-selected over training.
works.overlaps_component: C1 plus C2: parameter-level conflict-aware split, task-gated, in RL

works.title: Soft Conflict-Resolution Decision Transformer (SoCo-DT)
works.mechanism: Soft masks adjusted by Fisher information, using conflict and harmony scores per parameter; sparsity thresholds per task set by IQR.

works.title: Neuron-level Balance between Stability and Plasticity in Deep RL (NBSP)
works.mechanism: Identifies 'RL skill neurons' with a goal-oriented criterion, then protects them with gradient masking and experience replay.
works.overlaps_component: C4 neuron-level protection of reused skills while learning new ones
works.note: The identification rule and the numbers are not on the abstract page.

works.title: SSDE: Fine-Grained Sparse Network Allocation and Dormant Neuron Exploration for Continual RL
works.mechanism: Co-allocation under sparse coding splits parameters into frozen forward-transfer and trainable task-specific sets; dormant neurons found by sensitivity are reset to drive exploration.

works.title: Continual Task Allocation via Sparse Prompting (CoTASP)
works.mechanism: Sparse masks generated from a dictionary select a sub-network per task in a shared meta-policy; related tasks share more neurons.

works.title: Building a Subspace of Policies for Scalable Continual Learning (CSP)
works.mechanism: Grows a subspace of policies sublinearly in the number of tasks.

works.title: Same State, Different Task: Continual RL without Interference (OWL)
works.mechanism: Defines interference as the same observation being rewarded for different goals. Uses a shared trunk with a head per task, and picks a head with a bandit at test time.

works.note: Read from the PDF. This is 'reuse here, learn there' per state, at the action level.

works.mechanism: Trains a residual policy online on top of a large imitation-learned policy, with controlled exploration.
works.note: Whether the base is frozen and whether the residual is bounded is not stated on the abstract page.

works.note: Read from the PDF. ClonEx-SAC reaches 87% versus PackNet's 80%.

evidence_against_premise: Gradient conflict was not the bottleneck in multi-task RL once the baseline was stabilised. Kurin et al. (NeurIPS 2022), Meta-World MT10/MT50 with SAC: the plain sum of task losses, with a bigger replay buffer, actor L2 and fixed reward normalisation, is on par with PCGrad, MGDA, GradDrop and IMTL.

Capacity, especially critic capacity, explains most of the gains attributed to multi-task architectures. McLean et al. 2025: a plain baseline scaled to equal parameter count equals or beats Soft Modularization, PaCo and MOORE. Shrinking the critic (1024 to 400/200 wide) hurts a lot, while shrinking the actor does not. Splitting actor units may therefore target the wrong network.

Conflict shrinks with scale. BRC (2025) reports that 'the rate of gradient conflicts decreases as the number of parameters increases' and that gradient surgery 'might not be required after a certain model scale'. Meta-World+ (NeurIPS 2025) attributes MTMHSAC's decline with more tasks to network capacity.

Conflicts in gradient direction are not special to multiple tasks. Elich et al. (GCPR 2024, supervised): conflicts can be stronger between samples within a task than between tasks; multi-task learning is set apart by differences in gradient magnitude, which normalisation such as PopArt fixes rather than splitting.

Where RECON finds conflict depends mostly on the network architecture and stays consistent across datasets and training stages (ICLR 2023, supervised). A conflict map may reflect architecture more than task semantics.

At VLA scale the problem largely disappears. RLinf-VLA trains one OpenVLA-OFT model with GRPO to 98.11% on 130 LIBERO tasks (from 42%) and with PPO to 97.66% on 25 ManiSkill tasks. 'Simple Recipe Works' (RLC 2026) finds that sequential LoRA plus on-policy RL forgets less than 2% and beats parameter-isolation and regularisation baselines. Large forgetting appears only with SFT (78.7%), without LoRA (40.9%), or with a ~12M-parameter policy (11.4%). A growth method aimed eventually at VLAs therefore has weak motivation, and its case rests on small, from-scratch policies like ours.

For cold-start transfer (setting b), growth cannot supply the missing learning signal. Before the first success the advantages are critic noise (the morning doc: the first update of full fine-tuning moved 2.5 nats), so 'latent neighbours with opposite advantage' cannot be computed exactly when they are needed. Our G2′ found that cold-start conflict predictors from the source side do not beat simple heuristics (0/5).

Our own Stack data point to exploration, not representation conflict. While anchored, the deterministic policy already carries the cube to the goal, so the reused 'impressions' are fine. Success tracks whether the global gripper std snowballs (0.6 to 1.4) or collapses (0.6 to 0.4), not the gate labels. On T45, plain fine-tuning was best (AUC 0.93), so there was nothing to resolve.

In continual RL the critic, not the actor representation, carries most of the forward transfer. Wołczyk et al. 2022 also found that exploring with previous policies helps and that regularising the critic does not. Known fixes for collapse after transfer that involve no growth already exist: critic or value warm-up (VLA-RL, FORCE), LP-FT, BC/kickstarting retention (Wołczyk 2024), PEX, and residual policies (Policy Decorator).

The 'PCGrad but structural' framing is already taken: RECON pitches 'reduce conflicting gradients from the root', CoNAL (AAAI 2023) does conflict-triggered branching with Meta-World MT10 results, and HarmoDT/SoCo-DT do it per parameter in offline multi-task RL. Duplicating units from old units is DEN, splitting steepest descent and plasticity injection.

Duplicated units may simply not diverge. Drop-Upcycling (ICLR 2025) shows that experts copied from one dense layer specialise slowly unless partly re-initialised. Routers trained under RL also need special handling (arXiv 2510.23027, an LLM MoE paper; I read only the abstract).
open_gaps: Not found in my searches: conflict-triggered, state-gated (not task-gated) duplication of hidden units inside an on-policy RL actor. A partition-of-unity gate, h = (1−g(s))·u + g(s)·u', with u' copied from u, preserves the function at the moment of the split. Closest priors: Soft Modularization (learned per-state routing), CoNAL/RECON/DEN/HarmoDT (conflict-triggered but per task), splitting steepest descent (a unit split driven by the data, but averaged over the whole data distribution), and Munos & Moore / U-Tree (tabular). This is the only clearly open slot, and its novelty would be incremental.

Missing causal test in RL: conflict-selected versus randomly selected splits at equal parameter count. RECON has random-layer and random-parameter controls only for supervised learning; I did not verify whether CoNAL has one. Any paper needs this control plus an equal-parameter scaled baseline (McLean) and a learned-MoE baseline (Soft Modularization).

Suggested first test for setting (a), within the ~6 GPU-hour budget: on the unified multi-task PPO, compare (i) the lab baseline, (ii) a strong baseline at equal parameter count (critic at least 1024 wide, per-task PopArt, LayerNorm, learned task embedding), (iii) the strong baseline plus duplication of conflict-selected trunk units, and (iv) the strong baseline plus duplication of the same number of random units, with 2-3 seeds and shorter runs. Kill (a) if (ii) closes most of the 97.9% to 32-36% gap, or if (iii) minus (iv) is within seed noise.

Suggested test for setting (b): Pick to Stack fine-tuning from the source actor, with (1) value-only critic warm-up until the explained variance is positive, (2) a frozen trunk or a plasticity-injection head (h_θ + h_θ1' − h_θ2') until the first success, and (3) a state-dependent gripper std head in place of the global actor_logstd in /home/ryan/Documents/pve/wrwl/ppo.py. If this alone rescues fine-tuning (currently 0.002 AUC), the 'grow impressions' story is unnecessary for (b) and the contribution reduces to recipes that are already known.

Conflict as an exploration signal was not found as such; the nearest are QMP, ClonEx-SAC and SSDE's dormant-neuron exploration. It is only usable once the target task gives some signal. One cheap offline check needs no GPU: do 'opposite-advantage latent neighbours' carry any signal before the first success in the logged Stack runs? Our G2′ suggests not.

Null-space and gradient-projection protection (GPM, Adam-NSCL, TRGP, CUBER, InfLoRA) for on-policy, sparse-reward transfer: I found no RL evaluation in two searches, but such work may exist. The risk is that projecting away the source subspace also blocks exactly the conflicting behaviour (release) that must change.

Gaps in this sweep: for most 2025-2026 papers I read only abstracts (exact splitting rules and numbers for NBSP, SSDE, MoE-Loco, Mixture-of-World Models, PA-MoE, PhaseLoRA and IsCiL are unverified). LLM continual-instruction-tuning expansion methods were covered only through SETA. I did not identify the 'Dynamic Weight Expansion' baseline in 'Simple Recipe Works'. GradSplit is unverified (403). Memory Anchors comes from the lab's verified notes and was not reopened.

localize.summary:
Literature sweep (read-only; no project files edited, nothing run on GPU servers; PDFs fetched only to the scratchpad). I opened about 55 pages and report 51 works below; each entry's note says how much of the paper I read.

(1) LOCALIZING CONFLICT. Existing localizers work at several levels:
- per sample: gradient inner products (Bengio 2020); increase in TD error after an update (Liu 2023);
- per game segment (Fedus 2020) and per task stage (MENTOR);
- per layer (Recon) and per unit (DEN's weight drift);
- per state: Memory Anchors (latent kNN plus action disagreement), Gradient Coupling (similar states, interfering gradients, separate the embeddings), U-Tree/USM (split a state when return statistics differ), and the λ-discrepancy.

Every one of these detects CONFLICT through a new-task signal: rewards or TD targets, advantages, per-task gradients, or new-task demonstrations (Memory Anchors step 2, DEN labels). No surveyed work detects action conflict without new-task rewards or demos, which is our cold-start case. Only these are reward- and demo-free:
- representation overlap or novelty (Memory Anchors step 1 alone);
- parameter or neuron importance for the OLD task: EWC, MAS, and NBSP, which needs only old-task outcomes;
- output churn on reference states (CHAIN);
- generic aliasing penalties (DR3);
- the reward-free 'loop = bad' labels in Gradient Coupling.

All of these find overlap or importance, not conflict. In Memory Anchors' own ablation (LIBERO-Goal, NBT): full method .11, without the action-conflict step .13, MIR .14, random replay .18. So overlap alone already gives most of the gain (my calculation, about 70%).

Citing works of Memory Anchors: ACCRUE cites it only in related work and keeps the last N episodes by recency. Dream to Remember: abstract only (HTML 404). The other two citers I did not open. Nobody builds on its localization.

(2) EROSION DURING FINE-TUNING. The erosion is well documented:
- Wolczyk ICML'24: forgetting sits on 'Far' states that early fine-tuning does not visit. BC on old states works best; kickstarting fails when the pretrained policy is strong only on Far states; CKA shows early layers change fast at the start of fine-tuning.
- Ahn 2024: negative transfer is common in continual RL, worse for PPO, and plasticity fixes do not cure it; Reset & Distill wins.

Collapse at the start of fine-tuning is blamed on the critic or the optimizer, not on conflict, and the fixes are generic:
- PIRLNav: a random critic causes a rapid drop; fix is critic-only warmup, then critic-LR decay and actor-LR warmup.
- FLaRe: small LR, no entropy bonus, separate actor and critic; removing any one collapses Fetch to 0.
- WSRL: Q-function divergence; fix is warmup rollouts.

Policy reuse already has per-state copy gates (Q-filter, CUP, QMP, PEX), but they all need a critic trained on target rewards. Kickstarting, JSRL, TGRL and VLAJS cover anchor-then-release; JSRL's roll-in start states are next to our reset hard constraint, so avoid them.

VLA retention:
- With LoRA plus on-policy GRPO, VLAs barely forget (NBT 0.3, 1.0 and −2.4 on LIBERO-Spatial, -Object, -Long).
- Full fine-tuning (NBT 40.9) and a 12M-parameter policy (NBT 11.4) do forget.
- RL's Razor: forgetting tracks the KL to the base policy.

MULTI-TASK EVIDENCE. MTBench (massively parallel PPO) finds that gradient conflicts sit mainly in the critic. PCGrad and CAGrad do not beat vanilla on MT10, and critic-free GRPO beats PPO. McLean 2025: a scaled-up plain MLP matches MTRL architectures, and critic size matters most.

VERDICT.
- Setting (a): components (1) and (2) of the sketch are plausible but read as Memory Anchors + DEN/Recon + Gradient Coupling, and must first beat critic fixes, a wider network and MoE.
- Setting (b): the premise is contradicted by our own data and by the literature. Before the first success there is no conflict signal. The erosion we saw matches noise-driven updates (normalized advantages, KL early-stop off, 2.5 nats in the first update). After the first success, plain PPO learns release quickly. The bottleneck is exploration toward the first success, not representational conflict.

works.title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
works.setting: Continual imitation learning with replay; diffusion BC and pi0.5 on LIBERO; 2 real-robot suites
works.mechanism: Step 1: kNN distance quantiles in the old policy's observation latent plus 2-means pick new-task samples that fall onto the old-task manifold. Step 2: noise-and-denoise the new-task demo action with the old policy and keep samples whose disagreement exceeds mu + 2 sigma (conflict points). Step 3: replay the old samples nearest those points.
works.overlaps_component: (1) locate conflict in representation space; retention

Step 1 alone needs only new-task observations, but it finds overlap, not conflict. open_gaps: COLD-START CONFLICT IS UNIDENTIFIED. No surveyed method localizes ACTION conflict without new-task rewards or demonstrations. What is reward- and demo-free: Memory Anchors step 1 (overlap only), EWC/MAS/NBSP (old-task importance), CHAIN (churn), DR3 (generic aliasing). None of these says where the old action is wrong. Our own G2' (0/5 pairs) is consistent with this. A cold-start component must either be framed as protection plus exploration, or import a weak new-task signal: HER-style goal relabelling (as in the Q-filter paper), sub-goal predicates, a VLM judge, or a few target demos (as in Memory Anchors).

PRE-FIRST-SUCCESS EROSION IN PPO. Normalised advantages turn zero-variance returns into full-size noisy updates, and our KL early-stop is off, so the first update moved 2.5 nats. No robot-RL paper isolates this mechanism. The generic fixes all exist: critic-only warmup and actor-LR warmup (PIRLNav); small LR, no entropy bonus, separate actor/critic (FLaRe); a churn penalty (CHAIN); skipping zero-variance batches (DAPO); critic-free advantages (GRPO in MTBench, REINFORCE in RL's Razor). Any pilot must include these as baselines. If 'skip or shrink the actor update when a batch has no success, plus target_kl' removes the Stack erosion, component (2) has no job in setting (b).

STATE-LOCALISED PLUS UNIT-LOCALISED SPLITTING IN RL is not found in this sweep. Neighbours: DEN (unit drift, supervised), Recon (layer level, per-task gradients, supervised), NBSP (protects skill neurons, does not split), MoE/MENTOR/MOORE (learned routing), OWL (per-task heads), Gradient Coupling (separates embeddings). The combination looks open but will read as DEN + Recon + Memory Anchors. It must beat MoE and multi-head models, a wider MLP and a bigger critic (McLean 2025; MTBench).

SETTING (a): IS THE LAB DROP ACTOR ALIASING AT ALL? Nobody has checked whether the 97.9% to ~32-36% drop comes from actor aliasing or from the critic/value scale. MTBench (O3) and McLean point to the critic. Cheap diagnostic first: per-task actor vs critic gradient cosine (as in MTBench Fig. 6), then PopArt or per-task critic heads, a wider critic, and critic-free advantages. Only the drop that remains is a target for conflict-splitting.

TIMING CONFLICTS. Conflicts about WHEN to switch (release) are not caught by single-step action disagreement (Memory Anchors) or by an 'opposite advantage' test. The per-step advantage of holding one more step is tiny, and this is the same blind spot that made our value-based gold labels anchor the release region. Nothing in the sweep localizes such conflicts. The only related tools are global anneal or deactivation schedules (Kickstarting, TGRL, VLAJS).

CONFLICT-AS-EXPLORATION (component 3) was not found in this sweep, which was not a dedicated search. Adjacent: PEX (the frozen policy joins exploration via Q-softmax), QMP (other tasks' policies collect data). In cold start, conflict cannot be observed, so the exploration signal would need a proxy. One speculative option is the dimensions the source suppresses everywhere (the valid-action-suppression analog, e.g. gripper-open while grasping). Untested.

MEMORY ANCHORS HAS NOT BEEN MOVED TO RL. It assumes generative BC policies and new-task demos, and its citers (ACCRUE retains by recency; Dream to Remember, abstract only) do not use its localization. An on-policy Gaussian-PPO version could take new-task actions from the agent's own successful rollouts after the first success, but then it is a retention trick, not a way to learn faster.

VLA TRANSFER OF THE CLAIM. With LoRA plus on-policy RL, VLAs barely forget during sequential RL (Simple Recipe Works). The headroom lies in small policies, full fine-tuning, or joint multi-task RL. An 'eventually VLA' story needs a VLA setting that first shows measurable interference.
evidence_against_premise: OUR T45: plain fine-tuning (AUC 0.93, 2 seeds) beats every arm that protects or anchors the source (0.56-0.86). The source already succeeds 7% of the time; once the new task gives signal, PPO resolves the conflict itself, and protection only slows it.

OUR STACK: what decides the outcome is reaching the first success, not representational conflict. Within each group the deterministic policies are the same, and the seed decides whether gripper noise grows (about 0.6 to 1.4) or shrinks (to about 0.4). Runs whose training successes snowballed during the anchor learn release within 0.5M steps of the anchor ending. Before any success there is no gradient that could tell which units conflict, so growing or splitting units has nothing to act on.

OUR STACK, FULL FINE-TUNING: the erosion (lift 0.98 to 0.07) happened with KL early-stop disabled and normalised advantages on critic noise; the first update moved 2.5 nats. The literature attributes such early collapse to the critic and optimiser (PIRLNav, FLaRe, WSRL) and fixes it generically. This confound must be removed before blaming impression conflict.

OUR G2'/D1': source-side signals (familiarity, disagreement, |mu|^2) never beat trivial heuristics (0/5 pairs). On Stack the best source signal has AUROC 0.72, the same as the distance heuristic, and 'source progress' gets 0.54. The literature offers no better reward-free conflict detector.

OUR GOLD LABELS: value-based labels measured detour cost and marked 91% of near-goal states safe, which anchored exactly the release region. An 'opposite-advantage neighbours' detector is built from the same value signals and inherits this blind spot at timing decisions.

MEMORY ANCHORS' OWN ABLATION: dropping the action-conflict step costs little (NBT .13 vs .11 on LIBERO-Goal; random replay .18). On heterogeneous suites the method degenerates into filtered nearest-neighbour retrieval, and gains appear only with small buffers. 'Conflict' adds little beyond 'overlap'.

MULTI-TASK (a): MTBench finds gradient conflicts mainly in the critic. PCGrad (86.21) and CAGrad (82.98) do not beat vanilla MT-PPO (87.51) on MT10, while critic-free GRPO reaches 91.12 / 74.48 (MT10 / MT50). McLean 2025: a scaled-up plain MLP matches MTRL architectures and critic capacity matters most. Kurin 2022: plain summed losses are enough. Elich 2023: gradient-direction conflicts also occur in single-task learning.

REUSE CAN BE THE PROBLEM: Ahn et al. find fine-tuning from the previous network often gives negative transfer (worse for PPO), plasticity fixes do not cure it, and reset-and-distill wins. Wolczyk shows forgetting sits on Far states the new task does not visit early, not at conflict points, and generic BC on old states fixes it with no localization.

SCALE: at VLA scale with LoRA plus on-policy RL, sequential forgetting is about zero (NBT 0.3/1.0/-2.4), and the Fisher interference measure is 8x smaller than for a small policy (0.02 vs 0.16). The impression-conflict problem mostly belongs to small networks and full fine-tuning.

FOR THE PREMISE (for balance): forgetting concentrates in few task pairs (Memory Anchors). DQN interferes even when the input disambiguates the room, and separate features remove it (Liu 2023). MLP agents show conflict between stages of one task that MoE removes (MENTOR). Separating the embeddings of similar states with good and bad actions improves generalisation (Gradient Coupling). Small policies forget (NBT 11.4). Neuron-level protection works on Meta-World cycles (NBSP).

explore.summary:
Bottom line: I found no 2023-2026 paper that uses representation-space conflict between a reused policy and the new task (latent neighbours with opposite advantage or action) to steer exploration. In that exact form, component (3) of the sketch is open. The nearby literature is crowded, though, and its signals point the other way.

Closest works:
- Dodeja et al. 2025/26 turn the residual (and its SAC exploration) on only where the base policy is uncertain. Uncertainty is distance-to-data or ensemble variance, applied as a hard switch whose threshold decays.
- Yardimci & Cogurcu 2026 set a per-step noise multiplier in multi-task PPO of SmolVLA from two signals: random network distillation (RND) novelty on the action expert's hidden state, and critic competence (x0.4 for familiar and competent, x1.4 for novel and not competent). This stopped tasks from collapsing, but gave no gain over the BC baseline (Fisher p=0.40 at 3 seeds).
- BRPO's residual learns to reduce uncertainty where the belief over an expert ensemble has high entropy.
- MaxQInit (ICML 2018) is the tabular precedent for exploring where source values are refuted. It initialises Q optimistically as the max over past tasks' Q*.
- ADVISOR, A2T, CUP, QMP, CTPG and Energy-Based Transfer (EBT) gate reuse per state by imitability, attention, target-critic advantage, Q-switch or energy-based in-distribution score. All of them reuse where the prior is familiar or agrees, and fall back to RL elsewhere.

Every one of these signals is blind to the case that broke WRWL on StackCube: held-near-goal states are familiar to the PickCube source but need a different action (release). PARROT reports the same failure: a prior trained only on grasping failed on pick-and-place, likely because gripper opening never appeared in its data. A 'familiar-but-conflicting' signal is therefore the only real differentiator. Before the first success it can come only from the source side, for example the frozen source critic's TD error under the new reward. In-house D1' already found that source-side signals only tie simple heuristics (0/5).

On noise collapse under prior-regularised RL, the literature has global or inherited fixes, not conflict-localised ones:
- SPiRL auto-tunes the KL weight to a target divergence.
- Policy Decorator uses a bounded residual plus an epsilon ramp.
- RL Token uses an L2 anchor, a small fixed sigma and reference dropout.
- Warp RL (ManiSkill3, PPO) inherits the frozen base's state-dependent sigma(s). Exploration supplied independently of the base destabilised training.
- StructRL adds a noise budget and an anti-collapse regulariser. piRL and ReinFlow use learnable bounded noise.
- SimpleVLA-RL uses temperature 1.6, clip-higher and dynamic sampling. RPO and the LLM entropy papers (Cui 2025, Entropy-Preserving RL) are also global.
- GEB shows that exploration bonuses under a KL regulariser get pulled toward the reference's high-probability regions.

Rudner et al. (NeurIPS 2021) show that the gradient of a KL anchor scales as 1/sigma_ref^2. In /home/ryan/Documents/pve/wrwl/ppo.py (default copy_loss=rkl with the learner's log-std detached, lines 522-536), the mean pull is (mu - mu_src)/sigma_src^2. With source gripper std about 0.30, the anchor is stiffest on exactly the dimension that must change. The actor log-std is also one global parameter (lines 158-165), so exploration cannot currently be localised at all.

Cold-start erosion (fine-tuning destroying lift before the first success) has standard fixes that must be baselines:
- PIRLNav: critic-only phase, then the actor learning rate warmed up from 0.
- WSRL: warmup rollouts that recalibrate the critic.
- RIPT-VLA and SimpleVLA-RL: dynamic sampling that drops groups with uniform reward.
- Dark Room 2026: removing std-normalisation in all-fail groups.
Wolczyk et al. 2024 name the phenomenon (forgetting of pre-trained capabilities).

Components (1) and (2) are largely taken:
- Memory Anchors: conflict = representation overlap plus action disagreement, used to choose replay.
- Recon: high-conflict shared layers become task-specific copies.
- OWL, A2T, PEX and Neuroplastic Expansion grow or split modules.
- ZPRL (residual in a frozen policy's bottleneck latent) and RL Token already do representation-level reuse.

For setting (a), Kurin 2022, BRC 2025 and 'SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists' 2026 suggest the multi-task drop may come mostly from critic scale and normalisation rather than representational conflict.
