works.title: Policy and Value Transfer in Lifelong Reinforcement Learning (MaxQInit)
works.venue_or_id: ICML 2018, PMLR 80 (Abel, Jinnai, Guo, Konidaris, Littman)
works.mechanism: Initialise the new task's Q as the max over sampled past tasks' Q*. With high probability this upper-bounds the new Q* and so preserves PAC-MDP optimism. Sample complexity then counts only (s,a) where U(s,a) - V*(s) stays large, so exploration concentrates where past-task values overestimate the new task.
works.setting: Tabular lifelong RL; R-Max, Delayed-Q, Q-learning
works.overlaps_component: (3) value prediction error of source values in the new task
works.note: Mechanism verified from the PDF text (Alg. 1, Thm 3.7). Tabular precedent for 'explore where the source is refuted'. I found no deep-RL/PPO version that uses source-critic TD error in the new task as an exploration signal.

works.title: Bridging the Imitation Gap by Adaptive Insubordination (ADVISOR)
works.mechanism: w(s) = exp(-alpha * KL(pi_teach(s), pi_aux(s))), where pi_aux is trained by imitation only, on the shared representation. Loss = w*CE(teacher) + (1-w)*RL loss: imitate where imitable, use RL elsewhere.
works.setting: Gridworlds, multi-agent particle, 3D sims; privileged teacher
works.overlaps_component: WRWL per-state gate; (1) where copying fails
works.note: Learner-side per-state reuse gate that needs no reward success. It measures imitability under information asymmetry, not task conflict. Must-cite precedent for any per-state copy/learn weight.

works.title: Attend, Adapt and Transfer (A2T)
works.mechanism: Per-state softmax attention over frozen source solutions plus a base network learned from scratch. Attention moves to the base where sources are bad, which avoids negative transfer.
works.overlaps_component: (2) grow new capacity only where the reused one fails
works.note: Early 'reuse plus grow' architecture, gated per state but learned only from reward.

works.title: CUP: Critic-Guided Policy Reuse
works.mechanism: Per-state argmax of the soft advantage of source policies under the target SAC critic. Guidance KL weight beta_s = beta1 * min(A~, beta2*|V~|). Regularisation starts after 500k steps.
works.note: Needs an informative target critic, so it does not help before the first success (the cold-start case). Already listed as a baseline in the report.

works.title: QMP: Q-switch Mixture of Policies for Multi-Task Behavior Sharing
works.venue_or_id: ICLR 2025, arXiv 2302.00671 (Zhang, Jain, Hwang, Sun, Lim)
works.mechanism: For each task and state, pick the task policy whose mean action maximises the current task's Q, and use it only for off-policy data collection. The training objective is unchanged. It shares less from conflicting policies (Multistage Reacher).
works.setting: Meta-World MT10/MT50, Maze, Walker, Kitchen; SAC
works.overlaps_component: setting (a): cross-task behaviour sharing for exploration
works.note: Exploits agreement, not conflict. Off-policy only, so a PPO port would need importance weighting. Natural baseline for any multi-task exploration claim.

works.title: Efficient Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Cross-Task Policy Guidance (CTPG)
works.mechanism: A per-task guide policy picks, every K=10 steps, which task's control policy acts. Gates: allow policy j only if its guide-Q >= V_i(s); guidance only for tasks whose log-temperature is <= the average.
works.setting: Meta-World MT10/MT50, HalfCheetah MT5/MT8; SAC variants
works.overlaps_component: setting (a): exploration via other tasks' policies
works.note: MT10: MTSAC 62.72 -> 75.76, MHSAC 63.51 -> 74.94. MT50: SM 55.04 -> 66.24, PaCo 59.46 -> 68.10. No use of conflict; PCGrad appears only as a baseline.

works.title: Energy-Based Transfer for Reinforcement Learning

works.setting: Single- and multi-task RL (benchmarks not named on abs page)
works.overlaps_component: (3), opposite direction: suppress reuse out of distribution
works.note: Abstract only. Evidence that 'trust the prior where familiar' works, which is the opposite of 'explore where familiar but conflicting'.

works.title: Beyond Fine-Tuning: Transferring Behavior in Reinforcement Learning (Behavior Transfer)
works.mechanism: The pretrained policy is kept fixed. State-blind temporally extended 'flights' (start probability ~ log-uniform[0, 0.1], Zeta(2) length), plus an extra action a+ chosen by Q that samples one step from the pretrained policy.
works.note: Misaligned priors still helped exploration. Fine-tuned weights learned faster early but scored lower in misaligned games, and the authors hypothesise transferred representations are more robust to misalignment. Its exploration is not localised.

works.title: AC-Teach: Actor-Critic with Teacher Ensembles
works.mechanism: An ensemble of partial or contradictory teachers proposes actions. A Bayesian (DDPG) critic's probabilistic outcome estimates pick between teachers and the student to guide exploration.
works.note: Abstract only; the selection rule is not confirmed.

works.title: Guarded Policy Optimization with Imperfect Online Demonstrations (TS2C)
works.mechanism: Teacher-student shared control. Teacher interventions are based on trajectory-based value estimates, and the student can surpass an imperfect teacher.
works.note: Abstract only; the exact intervention rule is not confirmed.

works.title: Policy Decorator: Model-Agnostic Online Refinement for Large Policy Model
works.venue_or_id: ICLR 2025, arXiv 2412.13630 (Yuan, Mu, Tao, Fang, Zhang, Su)
works.mechanism: Residual SAC on a frozen BeT or diffusion policy. The residual is bounded to (-alpha, alpha) (alpha 0.03 for StackCube with BeT). Progressive exploration executes base+residual with probability epsilon, ramped 0->1 over H steps (1M for StackCube). The gate is state-independent.

works.title: Warp RL: Reshaping Base Policy Distributions for Dynamics Adaptation

works.title: Steering Your Diffusion Policy with Latent Space RL (DSRL)
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 2506.15799 (Wagenmaker et al.); CoRL 2025 per a PMLR listing seen in search (not opened)
works.mechanism: RL over the latent-noise space of a frozen BC diffusion policy, with black-box access only.
works.setting: Sim benchmarks, real robots, generalist policies
works.note: Abstract only. Exploration is limited to what the prior's noise space expresses.

works.title: Parrot: Data-Driven Behavioral Priors for Reinforcement Learning
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 2011.10024 (Singh, Liu, Zhou, Yu, Rhinehart, Levine)

works.title: Residual Skill Policies (ReSkill)
works.mechanism: A state-conditioned skill prior biases high-level exploration. A low-level residual adapts to variations outside the skill space.
works.overlaps_component: prior plus residual for out-of-prior variation
works.note: Abstract only.

works.title: Adaptive Skill Prior for Reinforcement Learning (ASPiRe)
works.mechanism: A library of specialised skill priors combined through an adaptive weight module and weighted KLs.
works.note: Abstract does not confirm per-state weighting.

works.title: On Pathologies in KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning from Expert Demonstrations
works.mechanism: A parametric Gaussian behavioural reference has small variance on demos and collapses to near zero elsewhere. The KL gradient grows as O(sigma0^-2), pinning the online policy to an unreliable mean. Flooring the variance (~1e-2) did not fix it. A GP reference, whose variance grows off-data, did.
works.overlaps_component: anchor stiffness and noise under prior-regularised RL
works.note: In our ppo.py the default rkl anchor (learner log-std detached) pulls the mean by (mu - mu_src)/sigma_src^2. Gripper sigma_src is about 0.30 (morning doc), so the anchor is stiffest on the release dimension.

works.title: General Exploratory Bonus for Optimistic Exploration in RLHF (GEB)
works.mechanism: Shows that exploration bonuses under KL or alpha-divergence regularisation bias exploration toward the reference's high-probability regions. Proposes a reference-dependent correction.
works.note: Warning for the sketch: an exploration signal added on top of a KL anchor gets pulled back to the prior's modes unless corrected.

works.title: SimpleVLA-RL: Scaling VLA Training via Reinforcement Learning
works.mechanism: GRPO with dynamic sampling (drop all-success and all-fail groups), clip range [0.8, 1.28], rollout temperature 1.6, no KL to a reference.
works.note: Exploration tricks gave 10-15% with no per-component breakdown. 'Pushcut' = the RL policy pushes the object instead of grasp-move-place. These are global fixes and the baseline any localised scheme must beat.

works.title: RIPT-VLA: Interactive Post-Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
works.mechanism: LOOP (RLOO advantage plus PPO clip). Dynamic rollout sampling discards contexts whose K rollouts all get the same reward. OFT actions are sampled from a Laplace with a learned scale head.
works.note: OFT reaches 97.5%. An SFT model at 4% reaches 97% from one demo within 15 iterations. Skipping no-signal batches is a direct fix for our 'full-size PPO steps on critic noise'.

works.title: VLA-RL: Towards Masterful and General Robotic Manipulation with Scalable RL
works.mechanism: Trajectory-level RL as multi-turn conversation, a VLM process reward model, critic warmup, curriculum.
works.note: Abstract only; no exploration mechanism described.

works.title: piRL: Online RL Fine-tuning for Flow-based Vision-Language-Action Models
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 2510.25889 (Chen, Liu, Zhang et al.; RLinf)
works.mechanism: Flow-Noise: a learnable, observation- and action-conditioned noise network (discarded after training). Flow-SDE: sigma_tau = a*sqrt(tau/(1-tau)).

works.title: ReinFlow: Fine-tuning Flow Matching Policy with Online RL
works.mechanism: A learnable noise network conditioned on observation, intermediate action and time, bounded by sigma_min and sigma_max. Entropy regulariser for state tasks.
works.note: 'When the success rate converges to 100%, the noise level naturally decays.' The same family collapsed the most tasks in 2609.28838.

works.title: StructRL: Structured Action-Space Exploration for Flow-Based VLAs
works.mechanism: Deterministic flow decoder. AR(1) temporally correlated noise on the action chunk. Group-aware (position/rotation/gripper), state-dependent bounded scales from an MLP, plus regularisers against collapse and over-amplification (dimension entropy, budget, smoothness).
works.setting: GR00T N1.5 / pi0 / pi0.5 on LIBERO, ManiSkill, CALVIN; real Franka
works.note: LIBERO 99.0 vs piRL 96.5 vs Gaussian 95.8. A budgeted, gripper-specific state-dependent scale is close to what a conflict-gated gripper noise would look like, but it is learned, not signal-driven.

works.title: Generalized State-Dependent Exploration (gSDE)
works.mechanism: Exploration noise is a function of state features, resampled periodically, for smooth exploration on real robots.
works.setting: PyBullet; real tendon robot, quadruped, RC car
works.note: Abstract does not give the formula.

works.title: Latent Exploration for RL (Lattice)
works.mechanism: Temporally correlated noise injected into the policy's latent activations gives correlated action noise (full covariance).
works.note: Precedent for perturbing 'impressions' rather than actions.

works.title: Dual-Flow RL with State-Aware Exploration (ECER)
works.mechanism: Entropy-Covariance Exploration Regulator: state-aware exploration from policy entropy and action-uncertainty covariance.
works.note: Abstract only; formula not confirmed.

works.title: Causal Influence Detection for Improving Efficiency in RL
works.mechanism: A situation-dependent causal action influence measure (conditional mutual information) detects states where the agent influences objects. Used to improve exploration and off-policy learning.
works.note: Region-restricted exploration (contact states) without any reused prior.

works.title: Robust Policy Optimization in Deep RL (RPO)
works.mechanism: Perturbed action distribution keeps PPO entropy from decaying.
works.note: Cheap global control for our gripper-std collapse.

works.title: The Entropy Mechanism of RL for Reasoning Language Models
works.mechanism: Empirical law R = -a*e^H + b. Entropy change tracks the covariance of log-prob with advantage. Clip-Cov and KL-Cov restrict updates on high-covariance tokens.
works.note: Same mechanism as our gripper std snowball: std grows or shrinks with the covariance between |a - mu| and advantage.

works.title: Beyond the 80/20 Rule: High-Entropy Minority Tokens Drive Effective RLVR
works.mechanism: Policy-gradient updates restricted to the top-20% entropy 'forking' tokens.
works.overlaps_component: focusing learning on a few decision points
works.note: +11.04 AIME'25 on 32B; training only on the low-entropy 80% hurts. A learner-entropy gate competes directly with a conflict gate.

works.title: Entropy-Preserving Reinforcement Learning
works.mechanism: REPO (advantage modification) and ADAPO (adaptive asymmetric clipping) to monitor and control entropy.

works.title: Targeted Exploration via Unified Entropy Control (UEC-RL)
works.mechanism: Extra higher-temperature rollouts only for 'difficult' prompts (zero positive rewards in the initial group), plus a replay-based entropy stabiliser.
works.overlaps_component: (3) concentrate exploration where the policy fails

works.title: Efficient Online RL Fine-Tuning Need Not Retain Offline Data (WSRL)
works.mechanism: A few warmup rollouts of the pre-trained policy recalibrate the offline Q-function before online updates, preventing a sudden value divergence.

works.note: Standard fix to try before blaming representational conflict.

works.title: PIRLNav: Pretraining with Imitation and RL Finetuning for ObjectNav
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 2301.07302 (CVPR 2023 not confirmed on abs page)
works.mechanism: Critic-only phase with the actor frozen, then the actor learning rate warmed up from 0 while the critic rate decays. This avoids 'destructive policy updates early on'.

works.title: Fine-tuning RL Models is Secretly a Forgetting Mitigation Problem

works.setting: NetHack, Montezuma's Revenge (Meta-World per search, not confirmed on abs)

works.mechanism: In all-fail groups, std normalisation divides tiny shaping-reward differences by a near-zero spread, giving full-size updates and collapse. Removing std normalisation alone restores parity with the baseline.

works.mechanism: Value = slow permanent part plus fast transient part.
works.overlaps_component: reuse plus grow in value space
works.note: Value-side analogue of 'share the rest, grow the conflicting part'.

works.title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
works.venue_or_id: arXiv 2608.26545 (Du, Sun, Xu, Shah, Itkina, Song); CoRL venue not shown on abs page
works.mechanism: Conflict = new-task observations collapsing onto old-task representations plus action disagreement (noise-and-denoise). Old data near the conflicts is replayed.

works.note: Component (2) at layer granularity, already done in supervised MTL (slight parameter increase). Per-unit, state-gated splitting in RL is the remaining delta.

works.title: Same State, Different Task: Continual RL without Interference (OWL)

works.title: Neuroplastic Expansion in Deep RL

open_gaps: Familiar-but-conflicting exploration is open. No paper I opened steers exploration toward states the reused policy finds familiar (overlap in its representation) where the new task needs a different action or has opposite advantage. Existing gates use novelty or epistemic uncertainty (Dodeja 2025/26, Yardimci & Cogurcu 2026, EBT) or Q-agreement (CUP, QMP, CTPG). They would leave the StackCube release region unexplored, because it is familiar to PickCube. This is the one real open slot for component (3).

A cold-start conflict signal for deep RL is missing. Before the first success there is no target advantage, so the signal must come from the source side. One option is the frozen source critic's TD error under the new reward: on held-at-goal states it predicts success while the new reward stays 0. MaxQInit is the only precedent (tabular, optimistic init); I found no deep-RL or PPO version. Risk: on T45-type tasks the source value is wrong almost everywhere, so the signal would be diffuse. In-house D1' already found source-side signals only tie simple heuristics.

Anchor-coupled exploration is missing. No prior-regularised method raises noise specifically where the anchor is active and the new task's return is flat. Current fixes are global (target-KL alpha in SPiRL, temperature and clip-higher in SimpleVLA-RL, RPO, the epsilon ramp in Policy Decorator) or inherited from the base (Warp RL). Normalising anchor stiffness is also untested for mean-only PPO anchors. Per Rudner, the pull scales as 1/sigma_ref^2; in ppo.py, rkl with the learner std detached pins the gripper mean about 1/0.30^2 = 11x per unit lambda.

Testbed prerequisite. In /home/ryan/Documents/pve/wrwl/ppo.py (lines 158-165) the actor log-std is one global nn.Parameter, so exploration cannot be localised at all today; the 0.6 -> 1.4 or -> 0.4 gripper std is one number for every state. Any test of component (3) first needs a state-dependent noise multiplier. Per 2609.28838, learned per-state noise trained by the policy gradient (ReinFlow-style) collapsed the most tasks. So use a non-learned, signal-driven multiplier with a fixed mean budget (StructRL-style).

The literature mostly lacks controls we will need. Only 2609.28838 partially checked whether a gain is just a different average noise. We need a matched-mean global-noise arm, a shuffled-signal arm (as in the WRWL label-shuffle), and at least 5 seeds on StackCube, given the coin-flip seed effect seen in-house.

Cheapest falsifier for component (3), within about 6 GPU-hours, not run because this task is read-only. On the StackCube kickstart arm, run 3 arms x 3-4 seeds. (A) Global gripper log-std floor or entropy bonus at the snowball level. (B) Gripper-noise multiplier that switches on where the gate is on and the source-critic TD error under the new reward is negative, with mean noise matched to A. (C) Same as B with a shuffled signal. If A is about equal to B, drop component (3). Keep the signal on noise only, never on resets or start states.

Setting (a) prerequisite. Before claiming representational conflict, measure whether the 97.9% -> 32-36% drop survives critic fixes: per-task PopArt, LayerNorm, a cross-entropy value loss, BRC-style task embeddings. On-policy (PPO) versions of QMP- or CTPG-style behaviour sharing do not exist; both are off-policy SAC. They would be the natural exploration baselines and could be a cheaper contribution.

Representation-level growth gated by conflict is untried. ZPRL perturbs a frozen policy's bottleneck latent globally, RL Token trains a head on a frozen readout, and Lattice injects latent noise. Nobody restricts a latent residual or new units to conflict states. This is open but incremental over ZPRL plus Recon, OWL and A2T.

Constraint hazard. PLD's hybrid rollouts (base for a random number of steps, then the residual) and JSRL's guide-rolled curricula decide where the learner starts acting. A conflict-chosen takeover point would effectively choose start states and violate the a2r boundary, so conflict should only modulate noise, gates or update weights.
evidence_against_premise: In-house (morning-2026-10-31.md): source-side cold-start signals only tied simple heuristics (D1' 0/5). Gold oracle labels anchored exactly the release region. StackCube outcomes were decided by the seed, through the global gripper std growing or shrinking, not by gate labels. On T45, plain fine-tuning from the source (AUC 0.93) beat every reuse arm. None of this shows that representational conflict is the bottleneck.

The gates that work in the literature do the opposite of the sketch for familiar states: trust the prior where it is familiar or confident, and add noise only where it is novel (Dodeja 2025/26; EBT; Yardimci & Cogurcu 2026, whose familiar-and-competent cell gets x0.4 noise).

Localised noise is not a free win. In Yardimci & Cogurcu 2026, uncertainty-gated noise prevented task collapse but gave no aggregate gain over the BC baseline (p=0.40, 3 seeds), and learned per-state noise collapsed 4-6 of 7 tasks per seed.

Exploration signals placed on top of a KL anchor are pulled back to the reference's modes (GEB, ICLR 2026). Rudner et al. show the anchor's stiffness is set by the reference variance, not by correctness. Both suggest the StackCube failure is about how the anchor is parameterised and scheduled (stiff 1/sigma_src^2 pull on the gripper, release only after lambda reaches about 0), which global fixes address. Examples: Policy Decorator's bounded residual plus ramp, RL Token's fixed sigma plus reference dropout, Warp RL's inherited sigma(s), SPiRL's target KL.

Cold-start erosion has standard optimisation fixes that do not involve conflict. Examples: PIRLNav's critic-only phase plus actor-LR warmup; WSRL's recalibration warmup; dynamic sampling that drops no-signal groups (RIPT-VLA, SimpleVLA-RL); removing std normalisation in all-fail batches (Dark Room 2026). Wolczyk et al. 2024 explain the erosion as forgetting of pre-trained capabilities.

For setting (a): Kurin et al. 2022 find that summing task losses with standard regularisation matches specialised multi-task optimisers, in RL too. BRC 2025 reduces interference with a high-capacity cross-entropy critic plus task embeddings and reaches state-of-the-art multi-task results. 'SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists' 2026 finds RL updates nearly orthogonal across tasks (LLM). The lab's 32-36% multi-task drop may mostly be critic scale or normalisation.

Components (1) and (2) are already done in close form. Memory Anchors localises conflict by representation overlap plus action disagreement. Recon splits high-conflict layers into task-specific copies. OWL, A2T, PEX and Neuroplastic Expansion grow or split modules. ZPRL and RL Token do representation-level reuse with residuals or heads. Novelty would rest on component (3), and on a cold-start signal that in-house data has not supported so far.

Behavior Transfer finds that misaligned pretrained policies help exploration even with state-blind random flights. Where exploration happens may matter less than having the prior's behaviours available, which weakens the case for conflict-localised exploration.

Competing explanation: a learner-entropy gate (Wang et al. 2025, top-20% high-entropy tokens) or a failure-triggered gate (UEC-RL) focuses learning on decision points without any reused-policy or conflict machinery. A conflict gate must beat these cheaper gates, not only global noise.

designs.name: CoFork: conflict-gated, function-preserving forks on frozen impressions
designs.one_line: Keep the source policy's impressions and behaviour frozen exactly. A latent cell gets a cloned copy of the top block, with its own exploration noise, only when the agent's own critic-free local policy-gradient test shows a consistent push away from the source there. The shared part is reused unchanged, and each conflict is resolved by separate parameters rather than by projecting gradients (PCGrad) or by anchoring (WRWL).
mechanism: 1. Build the agent (new module wrwl/fork.py, class ForkAgent). Load the source actor (actor_mean.* from --init_ckpt) as a frozen network S = [L1, tanh, L2, tanh | L3, tanh | L4]. The trunk T = S[:4] gives h2, Top = S[4:6] gives the impression z (last hidden layer, 256-d), and R = S[6] gives mu_src. The fork F = deepcopy(S[4:]) (L3', tanh, L4') is trainable; --fork_depth 1 clones only L4. The critic is fresh, as with --init_actor_only. Every arm gets a global log-std l_g reset to -0.5; Stack arms also get a gripper-std floor of 0.6. A trainable fork log-std offset dl starts at +0.5.

2. Policy. Under no_grad compute h2 = T(x), z = Top(h2), mu_src = R(z). Then mu_F = F(h2), and the gate is g(x) = sum_k open_k * softmax_k(-||z - c_k||^2 / tau), computed without gradient. The mean is mu = mu_src + g * (mu_F - mu_src), and log sigma = l_g + g * dl. F starts as an exact clone, so opening a cell leaves the mean unchanged (function-preserving). F receives gradient only through g > 0, so updates stay inside open cells, and every ungated state keeps the source's action exactly (no erosion). This is the per-state version of the frozen-trunk smoke test, whose first update moved 0.02 nats/decision against 2.4 for full fine-tuning.

3. Cells. After the first rollout, run k-means on the batch's z (K0 = 32, 10 Lloyd steps on GPU). Set tau = 0.25 x the median squared distance to the nearest centroid. Every 10 iterations, if more than 5% of states lie beyond the initial 95th-percentile distance, add 4 centroids by k-means on those states (cap 64). Centroids never move: the gate is defined on a frozen latent, so it is stationary.

4. Critic-free local signal, computed after the rollout and before the PPO epochs. Use truncated discounted returns inside the rollout window, G_t = r_t + gamma * (1 - dones[t+1]) * G_{t+1}, with no critic and no bootstrap. Subtract a leave-one-out per-cell baseline b_i. The per-sample desired mean update is v_i = (G_i - b_i)(a_i - mu_i) / sigma_i^2 (8-d, rollout policy, unclamped actions). By Stein's lemma, E[v | s] = dE[G | s]/dmu, so v is an unbiased local policy gradient, and it is identically 0 until a reward is observed. GAE advantages inherit the critic's spatial noise, because actions change V(s'); that noise drove the 2.5-nat first fine-tune update on Stack. v cannot open forks on it.

5. Test per cell k. Aggregate v into blocks, one per (env, iteration) restricted to the cell (scatter_add on env*K + k), and pool the last W = 5 iterations. The statistic is T_k = sum_d (sum_b m_bd)^2 / sum_b m_bd^2; its denominator is invariant to sign flips. The p-value comes from 2,000 random sign flips of whole blocks. A cell passes when it has at least 30 blocks and p < 0.001 on 3 consecutive iterations. Among passing cells, open at most 4 per iteration, in decreasing T_k. With strong (dense) signal this becomes conflict-ordered progressive unfreezing. Cells never close, and the test is skipped while the window contains no rewarded episode.

6. PPO itself is unchanged: GAE, clip, value loss, normalised advantages. The optimiser holds F, dl, l_g and the critic. Each iteration, write to fork.csv the open cells, the gated fraction E[g], the fork std, the per-cell p-values, and the phase or region of the gated states. Save the gated-fraction schedule for the matched-random control.

7. Controls run on the same code path:
- --fork random opens random unopened cells (weighted by visitation) until the gated fraction matches the paired detect run's schedule.
- --fork all opens every cell from iteration 1, which amounts to a frozen lower trunk plus a trainable top block.
- --fork hand sets g = 1 when the TCP-cube distance exceeds 5 cm: learn the approach, keep the contact. This is the structural twin of M1's best hand gate on T45.
- --fork oracle (Stack only) opens cells up front where conflict_probe's two experts disagree in gripper sign. This is the structural twin of the main agent's conflict-gated anchor.
- --fork_dlogstd 0 removes the fork-local noise.

8. Multi-task extension (setting a). Define cells on a fixed representation: a frozen pretrained or source latent, or the normalised input for from-scratch runs. Index forks by (task, cell). Open task t's fork in cell k only when (i) its block-mean update there is significant and (ii) its inner product with the other tasks' pooled update in k is significantly negative, using the same sign-flip test on the inner product. Task t's samples in k then route through its own clone. That conflict leaves the shared parameters, while every other (task, cell) pair keeps sharing. This is structural PCGrad at task x state-cell granularity.
how_it_differs: PCGrad and its relatives (CAGrad, Nash-MTL, FAMO) keep one set of shared parameters and remove the conflicting component of a gradient every step, so both updates are truncated and the shared weights keep absorbing the conflict. CoFork never edits the shared impressions. A conflicting cell gets its own cloned parameters, so 'keep the source here' and 'learn the new action there' are both satisfied exactly, and conflict is detected per latent cell, not per task.

RECON, GradPS and DEN split layers, neurons or units when conflict is triggered, gated by task or agent group everywhere (RECON and DEN are supervised; GradPS is value-based MARL). CoFork splits by state cell inside a single new task, and by task x cell in MT. It keeps sharing outside the conflict cells and is function-preserving at the moment of the split.

PNN, plasticity injection and LoRA add capacity that acts on every state (a column per task, a global injected head, a global low-rank update), so new-task updates move behaviour everywhere, much like the global readout in the main agent's frozen-trunk arm. CoFork's capacity is confined to detected cells, and untouched cells reproduce the source exactly.

MoE routers (Soft Modularization, MOORE, SDP, DyGRO-VLA's residual experts) and per-state retrieval (IsCiL) are either learned end to end, which is noisy under sparse RL, or keyed by task or retrieval. None of them opens capacity because a conflict was detected. CoFork's router is a fixed partition of the frozen latent whose cells are opened only by a statistical test.

Memory Anchors localises conflict in the old latent using new-task demonstrations and fixes it with replay. CoFork localises without demonstrations, from the agent's own advantage-weighted action deviations, and fixes it with structure.
closest_prior: PEX, Policy Expansion for offline-to-online RL (ICLR 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00935. Frozen old policy plus a new one, chosen per state by Q-softmax; the new policy is randomly initialised and trained off-policy. (survey-verified)

Dodeja et al., Accelerating Residual RL with Uncertainty Estimation (2025/26), https://arxiv.org/html/2506.17564v2. A SAC residual acts only where base uncertainty exceeds a decaying threshold. (survey-verified)

PARTS, From Pretraining to Proficiency (arXiv 2609.21788, Sep 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21788. Frozen base with bounded residuals only at human-identified bottleneck subtasks, gated by agent-generated selectors; full-task success 32% to 61% and 50% to 95%. I opened the abstract; the selector mechanism is unverified.
Memory Anchors (arXiv 2608.26545), https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26545. Conflict cells found in the old latent plus action disagreement (needs demos); the remedy is replay. (local verified notes)

RECON (ICLR 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.11289, and GradPS (ICML 2025), https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/qin25c.html. Conflict-triggered layer or neuron clones gated by task or agent group. (survey-verified; I opened the GradPS abstract page at mlanthology)

DEN, https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01547; plasticity injection (NeurIPS 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15555; PNN, https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04671. Growth or duplication with protection, but per task or global. (survey-verified)

Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in RL (NeurIPS 2026, NVIDIA), https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/publication/split_rl.html. Gradient-boosted trees with guidance labels route locally conflicting updates into disjoint state regions; the page argues that neural nets lack such a mechanism. Constrained and offline RL. Project page only; no arXiv yet and no numbers, so details are unverified.
Soft Modularization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.13661, and IsCiL, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.22658. Per-state routing, learned or retrieval-keyed, and not triggered by conflict. (survey-verified)

pilot.setting:
Stage A is the decisive, low-noise stage (about 1.4 GPU-h). PushCubeDir from the official PushCube expert S0 (runs/experts/runs/PushCube/final_ckpt.pt), --init_actor_only, 2048 envs x 20 steps, stop at eval 0.9. Three settings:
- T45 dense: gamma 0.8, M1 config, cap 3M. M1 found a local conflict here: copying the source only near contact reached 80% at 0.25M, against 1.31M for scratch and 0.49/0.90M for finetune.
- T90 dense, cap 3M: checks that CoFork never transfers negatively.
- T45 sparse: gamma 0.95, --bootstrap_at_done=truncated, --target_kl=1e9, step-3 config, cap 4M.
Stage B (Stack, about 2.0 GPU-h) runs only if Stage A criteria 1, 3 and 4 pass. StackCubeNarrow sparse from PickCube_wc_s1 via --obs_adapter=stack_to_pick, with the run_pilot_reuse.sh settings (1024 x 50, gamma 0.95, halt at 15M). Every Stack arm gets the std reset and a 0.6 gripper-std floor, so exploration noise is identical across arms. This also removes the std-collapse coin flip, which makes 5 seeds enough.
Queue behind runs/pilot (which holds 3 lanes) with scripts/with_gpu_mem.sh. Seeds: 3 per push setting, 5 on Stack.
arms: scratch (dense settings only; T45-sparse scratch is already known to be 0)
ft: source actor including its log-std, equal to the step-3 finetune arm. M1's finetune also loaded the theta=0 critic, a confound this pilot removes.
ft-reset: source actor with the log-std reset to -0.5
frozen-readout: --freeze_trunk plus std reset. The global readout learns; this is the main agent's frozen arm with the std controlled.
CoFork: detected cells, fork depth 2, dl = +0.5
CoFork-random: the paired CoFork run's gated-fraction schedule, filled with random cells
CoFork-all: every cell open from iteration 1 (frozen lower trunk plus trainable top block)
CoFork-noise0: detected cells with dl = 0 (push only; separates structure from fork-local exploration)
CoFork-hand: fork where the TCP-cube distance exceeds 5 cm (both T45 settings; an expert-designed reference)

Stage B: frozen-readout, CoFork and CoFork-random, 5 seeds each. Optionally CoFork-oracle (3 seeds, +0.4 GPU-h) to compare hard isolation with the main agent's conflict-gated anchor under the same localisation. The existing runs/pilot frozen_boost arm serves as the oracle-noise reference.
pilot.success:
Stage A passes on criteria 1, 3 and 4; criterion 2 is reported as a safety check.
1. T45 dense: CoFork's median steps-to-80% is at most 0.6 x ft-reset and at most 0.5 x scratch, and every CoFork seed is faster than every ft-reset seed.
2. T90 dense: CoFork is no slower than min(scratch, ft-reset), i.e. no negative transfer.
3. In every setting where CoFork's final gated fraction is at most 0.5, CoFork is at most 0.75 x CoFork-random and at most 0.8 x CoFork-all, with all seeds ordered.
4. No cell opens before the first rewarded episode in any sparse run.
Stage B passes when all of these hold:
- at least 4 of 5 CoFork seeds reach 0.8 by 15M, while frozen-readout and CoFork-random reach it in at most 2 of 5 (or their KM median time is at least 1/0.6 of CoFork's);
- the deterministic lift rate stays at least 0.9 at every checkpoint before the first success in all CoFork seeds;
- at least 60% of the gated mass lies in the 'held, <= 2.5 cm' and 'released near goal' phases.

risks: Structure does not solve cold start. Before the first reward no cell can open, so on Stack CoFork still depends on the shared, floored gripper noise to get its first successes; structure can only stop erosion and speed learning afterwards. If those first successes are the whole problem, CoFork equals frozen-readout (kill). An optional cold-start seed would open cells where the frozen source critic is in its top 5%, i.e. states the source treats as done. That overlaps with the exploration designer's 'familiar but refuted' signal and belongs in that pilot.

With strong or dense signal, almost every cell becomes significant. The cap of 4 openings per iteration turns this into conflict-ordered progressive unfreezing. But if the conflict is global, CoFork reduces to top-block fine-tuning. Global conflict is likely on T90/T180, and conflict_probe found arm-joint 'style' gaps of 1.3-2.2 std even where both experts are just reaching.

Detection latency. Critic-free truncated returns are high-variance, and the test needs 3 consecutive hits. On easy pairs CoFork may therefore lose to ft; on T45 sparse, ft already reaches 80% in about 1M steps.

Cells are defined on the source's own impressions. If the source maps states that need different actions into one cell, the cell mixes 'keep' and 'change' states, and CoFork either erodes part of the cell or misses the conflict. An example is the near-grasp phase, which keeps a 0.70/0.96 residual on frozen Pick features in conflict_probe. That case needs AliasGrow.
A single fork shared by all open cells couples distinct conflict regions again. Per-cell forks fix this at a higher parameter cost.
The gain may come from fork-local noise (+0.5 log-std where forks open), i.e. from exploration rather than structure. The CoFork-noise0 ablation is required before making any structural claim.

Novelty is incremental, about 4/10 by my estimate. Every ingredient exists: PEX, Dodeja et al., PARTS, Memory Anchors, RECON/GradPS, plasticity injection and our own WRWL gate. The defensible differences are the function-preserving clone, a local test that cannot fire before any reward, and a matched-random-locality control that none of these papers report. Split-RL (NeurIPS 2026, trees) claims that neural networks lack local conflict isolation. CoFork is a neural answer to that claim, but reviewers will compare against it once its arXiv appears.
Another agent is editing wrwl/ppo.py at the same time, so edits can collide.
designs.vla_path:
Treat the frozen SFT VLA as the source: pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT in RLinf, or GR00T N1.5 as in PolicyWeave.
- Forks are LoRA adapters with B = 0 at birth (function-preserving) on the last k blocks of the action expert or head.
- They are gated per action chunk by soft assignment of the frozen action-expert hidden state, pooled over the chunk, to K k-means prototypes from rollouts; for multi-task, the gate is also indexed by instruction id.
- The detector is the same sign-flip test on block-averaged score-function updates of the chunk mean, using Monte Carlo GRPO/PPO advantages. For flow-matching heads, use the Gaussian step log-prob of Flow-Noise or Flow-SDE.
Ladder:
1. This pilot.
2. RLinf PPO on OpenVLA-OFT on the ManiSkill pick-place suite (RLinf-VLA, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06710, reports 28% to 97.7% with global LoRA). Compare global LoRA with CoFork-LoRA on sample efficiency and on retention of untouched tasks and phases.
3. LIBERO-Goal (same scene, different instructions, i.e. real aliasing). Start with a premise check: joint versus per-task RL at matched steps. The evidence is mixed. PolicyWeave (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33125v1, opened) reports 60.7% for joint RL against 74.1% for merged task-specific RL experts on 18 RoboCasa365 tasks. DyGRO-VLA (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.17486v1, opened) reports negative Open/Close gradient cosine under a shared head, and collapse of LoRA-on-VLM in multi-task online RL. But RLinf reaches about 98% on LIBERO-130 jointly, and Simple Recipe Works finds that LoRA plus on-policy RL barely forgets.
4. Only if a gap exists: CoFork-LoRA gated by (instruction, cell) against global LoRA, per-task LoRA (CORAL-style), DyGRO-style residual MoE, and PolicyWeave-style merge-later.

designs.name: AliasGrow: grow new impressions only where the old ones alias
designs.one_line: Freeze the source's impressions. Whenever the new task's critic-free desired action updates cannot be expressed by any readout of those impressions, as judged against a block-permutation null, add a few hidden units. Their input directions are TINY's closed-form solution for that residual, and they start with zero output weights, so behaviour is unchanged at birth. Conflicting states are then separated by new impressions instead of by overwriting or projecting the shared ones.
mechanism: 2. Every C = 5 iterations, if the pooled window contains reward signal, compute the critic-free desired update v_i as in CoFork step 4, with a batch-mean baseline. It is unbiased, and it is zero before any reward.

3. Remove what the current structure can already absorb. Ridge-regress v on phi = [z; m*u; 1] with lambda = 1e-3 n, and take the residual r_i = v_i - B phi_i. The residual is the part of the desired update that no readout of the current impressions can express: states whose impressions coincide but whose desired actions differ (the aliasing conflict). It is the regression form of 'latent neighbours with opposite advantage'.

5. PPO trains R', V, the active rows of A and b, the critic and the log-std. Growth stops at 64 units. Log the units added, the residual energy they explain, and the phase or region where each new unit's activation variance is concentrated.

7. Multi-task extension (setting a):
- fit one shared readout update on pooled tasks and take the per-task residuals r_t;
- grow task-gated units (active only on task t's samples) from the SVD of task t's residual-input cross-covariance.
Capacity is added only in the input directions where the shared impressions cannot serve task t. This answers task-gradient conflict structurally instead of with PCGrad's projection. Controls: random task-gated growth, multi-head readouts, and a shared actor of 2x width at matched parameters.
how_it_differs: PCGrad resolves conflicting gradients by discarding the component of one gradient along another. AliasGrow resolves the conflict at its source: two state sets that the shared impressions map to the same code but that need different actions. It adds the representational directions that separate them, so both desired updates become expressible and neither is truncated.

TINY, GradMax, SENN and splitting steepest descent are supervised growth criteria for networks trained from scratch. AliasGrow transplants the expressivity-bottleneck criterion into on-policy RL on top of a frozen, transferred network. It handles policy-gradient noise with a critic-free desired update and a block-permutation null, and it uses growth to resolve transfer and multi-task conflict rather than to save compute.
Neuroplastic Expansion and GrowNN grow RL networks for plasticity or capacity, globally and starting from a small network. They have no frozen source and no conflict criterion.

RECON, DEN and PTSL add task-specific capacity: RECON duplicates layers, DEN duplicates units, and PTSL adds dense task-specific corrections on top of a common policy (exact layer structure not checked). AliasGrow instead adds new directions computed from the residual, not copies of old units, leaves every old unit untouched, and needs no task identity in single-task transfer.

Gradient Coupling and our backup topic 'Aliased, Not Overloaded' separate aliased embeddings by changing the shared representation with an auxiliary loss. AliasGrow keeps the old impressions intact and adds new ones, so nothing the source already does well can be eroded.

GradientSpace (LLM instruction tuning) clusters samples in gradient space and trains one LoRA expert per cluster behind a learned router. AliasGrow needs no clustering and no router, and it adds individual units in closed form.
closest_prior: TINY, Growing Tiny Networks (TMLR 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19816. Detects expressivity bottlenecks from the functional gradient and adds neurons in closed form (sigma linearised, two SVDs, per https://growingnet.github.io/growing_wiki/algorithms/tiny.html). CIFAR only; no RL. (I opened the abstract and the wiki.)

Self-Expanding Neural Networks, https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04526. A natural-gradient expansion score decides when and where to add width or depth; classification and regression only. (I opened the abstract.)
GradMax (ICLR 2022), https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05125, and splitting steepest descent (NeurIPS 2019), https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02366. (survey-verified)

Neuroplastic Expansion (ICLR 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07994: RL growth from potential gradients plus dormant-neuron pruning. GrowNN, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11706: function-preserving layer growth in RL. (survey-verified; Neuroplastic Expansion's method details come from search snippets)

RECON (ICLR 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.11289; DEN, https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01547; PTSL, Projected Task-Specific Layers (ICRA 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08776, which pairs a common policy with dense task-specific corrections on MT10/MT50. (I opened the PTSL abstract; its exact layer structure is unverified.)
Gradient Coupling (arXiv 2509.23870), https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23870. Separates the embeddings of similar states with good and bad actions via an auxiliary loss. (survey-verified)
GradientSpace (arXiv 2512.06678), https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06678. Clusters samples in gradient space into LoRA experts behind a router, for LLM SFT. (I opened the abstract.)

API, Adaptive Plasticity Improvement for Continual Learning (CVPR 2023), https://mlanthology.org/cvpr/2023/liang2023cvpr-adaptive. Measures plasticity for each new task and improves it when needed. The mechanism, including whether it adds dimensions, is unverified because the PDF returned 403.

pilot.setting:
Stage 0 runs offline (about 0.2 GPU-h) and decides whether RL is worth running at all. Extend scripts/conflict_probe.py to the pairs S0 -> T45/T90/T180, using M1's scratch seed-1 checkpoints as target experts and the PullCube expert as a second T180 target, alongside a rerun of Pick -> Stack with saved states. On the visited states:
- fit a ridge readout of the target expert's actions on the frozen source z;
- add 32 units in 4 rounds of 8, using TINY's closed form on [x; h1], versus 32 random units;
- compare held-out R^2 gains overall and by phase.
Stage 1 tests the multi-task premise (about 0.75 GPU-h). Use PushCubeDir with a per-env direction theta in {0, 90, 180, 270}, balanced by env index, with the goal visible plus a 4-d task one-hot; dense reward, gamma 0.8, 2048 x 20, 8M steps. Compare joint MT-PPO, joint MT-PPO with per-task critic heads and per-task advantage normalisation, separate actors with a shared critic, and single-task runs at matched per-task steps.
Stage 2 tests transfer (about 0.55 GPU-h). T90 and T180 dense from S0 (init_actor_only), cap 3M. The scratch, ft-reset and frozen-readout runs on T90 are shared with the CoFork pilot. Reset & Distill found that PPO fine-tuning often transfers negatively and that plasticity fixes do not cure it, but it never tested a std reset; ft-reset settles that question on our pairs.
Stage 3 (about 0.8 GPU-h) runs MT-AliasGrow on the 4-direction suite, and only if Stage 1 shows an actor-side gap.
arms: Stage 0: frozen-z readout; + 32 TINY units; + 32 random units; random-network features; raw state
Stage 1: single-task runs for each of the 4 directions; joint MT-PPO; joint + per-task critic heads and per-task advantage normalisation; separate actors + shared critic
Stage 2: scratch; ft-reset; frozen-readout; AliasGrow; AliasGrow-rand (paired schedule, random directions); LoRA-matched (rank 16 on frozen L2 and L3)
Stage 3 (conditional): MT-AliasGrow (task-gated grown units); random task-gated growth; multi-head readouts; shared actor of 2x width at matched parameters

risks: Policy-gradient noise. Even with the block-permutation null, the residual SVD may be dominated by noise and growth may rarely fire, which collapses AliasGrow to frozen-readout.

Random features are already strong. In conflict_probe, a random 3x256 network gives readout R^2 0.84/0.80, against 0.94/0.92 for the Pick features. GrowNN reports that even random growth beats static networks. Targeted and random growth may therefore fall within seed noise; Stage 0 tests this cheaply with oracle targets.

TINY's directions are first-order (tanh linearised at 0), and the new units act globally. Localised nonlinear residuals may be missed, and the learned outputs of new units act on every state, which brings interference back. A CoFork-gated variant would restore locality, at the cost of combining two mechanisms.

The negative transfer AliasGrow targets may be an artefact: M1's finetune loaded the theta=0 critic and the source's small std. With init_actor_only and a std reset, there may be no gap to close on T90/T180.

Novelty is incremental, about 3.5/10. Growth criteria (TINY, GradMax, SENN), RL growth (Neuroplastic Expansion, GrowNN) and task-specific capacity (RECON, DEN, PTSL) all exist. The difference lies in the frozen-source transfer use, the critic-free desired update with a permutation null, and the targeted-versus-random control in RL.

designs.name: SEAM: explore at the seam where the reused skill thinks it is done
designs.one_line: Before the first success, move the exploration budget to states where the frozen source actor's own hidden layer says 'my task is finished' but the new task has paid nothing. Keep the reused trunk frozen and the noise at source level everywhere else. The boost fades by itself as the new critic learns.
mechanism: 1. Reuse and protect. Start the actor from the source (--init_ckpt=PickCube_wc_s1 --init_actor_only) and freeze its three hidden layers (--freeze_trunk, /home/ryan/Documents/pve/wrwl/ppo.py:318-321). Only the 8x256 readout and actor_logstd learn. The reused 'impression' is h(s) = agent.actor_mean[:-1](s). In the main agent's smoke test, freezing cut the first update from 2.4 to 0.02 nats per decision.

2. Done-probe, fitted offline from the source alone (new scripts/seam_probe.py; needs no target reward, demos or target expert). Roll the source expert in its own task (PickCube-v1, robot_uids=panda_wristcam, 512 envs x 50 steps, sampled actions). In each episode whose first success is at step t*, label h(s_t) positive if t >= t*-4 (arriving at the goal and holding still) and negative if t <= t*-10. Fit a ridge-logistic probe d(s) = sigmoid(w.(h-mu)/sd + b) and calibrate it to source-side recall >= 0.9. More general variant: d(s) = the source task's own success test read through the adapter. For Pick->Stack that test is PickCube's is_obj_placed (cube within 2.5 cm of the goal) plus grasped, which is exactly the region of the main agent's --explore_boost (ppo.py:176-180, minus the robot-static clause). That region is therefore already label-free for this pair, not an oracle.

3. Offline locator check (same script, no RL). Re-roll the Pick and Stack experts in StackCubeNarrow-v1 exactly as /home/ryan/Documents/pve/scripts/conflict_probe.py does. Report the AUROC of d(s) against the per-state sign disagreement between the two experts' gripper commands. Also report coverage f, the share of Pick-in-Stack states with d > 0.5. Pass: AUROC >= 0.85 and f <= 0.6.

4. Exploration-yield check (new scripts/seam_yield.py, no training, about 0.1 GPU-h). Run the frozen source policy in Stack for 4096 episodes under each noise layout used in the pilot. Record the success, release-at-goal and carry-drop rates. This settles 'does placement matter' with thousands of episodes, so it is not subject to the seed coin flip. Gate: the seam layout's success yield must be >= 3x the global-matched layout's.

5. Seam gate at rollout time: g(s) = d(s) * (1 - clamp(V_hat(s), 0, 1)). V_hat is the learner's own critic, which under --bootstrap_at_done=truncated is a discounted success probability. g is a conflict between what the reused representation predicts ('done') and what the new task returns (no reward). It is defined before the first success, where advantage-based conflict tests have nothing to work with. In the rollout, compute the value, then g, then sample (replaces the single call at ppo.py:436). Store g in a new buffer gates[num_steps, num_envs].

6. State-dependent noise inside the policy. Agent.dist(x, g) returns logstd = actor_logstd + beta * g[:, None], with beta = (0,...,0, 1.2), i.e. the gripper only. A general option is to boost only dimensions where the source mean is saturated (|mu_src| > 0.9), the suppressed action. Sampling, stored log-probs, the PPO ratio (pass g=b_gates[mb] at ppo.py:503) and the KL log (ppo.py:548) all use the stored g, so the boost is part of the policy distribution, as --explore_boost already is. The deterministic evaluation is unchanged.

7. Self-annealing, and no anchor. When seam states start leading to success, V_hat rises there and the boost fades, so precision is not paid for later. There is no KL term, so the release dimension is never pinned with a 1/sigma_src^2-stiff pull. There are no resets and no change of start states (a2r boundary): the gate only changes the noise scale of the one on-policy policy.

8. Optional protection for unfrozen variants (VLA path). Skip the policy-gradient term on rollout batches with zero successful episodes (critic-only update, DAPO-style). This stops normalised advantages on critic noise from eroding the reused readout before the first success.
how_it_differs: Dodeja et al. (uncertainty-gated residual) explore where the base policy is unfamiliar or uncertain, and state that when the base is certain it is also correct. The Stack seam is familiar, certain and wrong. SEAM targets familiar states that are finished but refuted.

Yardimci & Cogurcu 2026 scale noise by RND novelty x critic competence, giving x0.4 noise where states are familiar and competent. Their applied noise stayed within 0.006-0.015 of the fixed scale, no arm beat BC, and the noise was not localised by phase. SEAM's signal is refuted done-ness, not novelty, and its pilot isolates placement with matched-budget and misplaced controls.
TMRL learns a per-state noise level with a high-level SAC policy from reward, which gives no signal before the first success. SEAM places noise without any target reward.

Skill chaining (Bagaria & Konidaris), PLD's random takeover and JSRL's guide roll-in hand control to another policy at a boundary or a random time, or choose start states. SEAM keeps one PPO policy with no handover and no start-state choice; only sigma(s) changes.

WRWL / step 3 anchored the mean to the source with value labels that measure detour cost, and the gripper std stayed at the source's 0.30. SEAM never anchors. It spends exploration exactly at the release decision those runs could not reach.

Main agent's frozen_boost pilot uses the same mechanics with a hand region and an additive boost. SEAM adds a source-only locator that transfers to settings without a success test (real robots, VLAs), and adds the controls that separate placement from amount of noise.

Stage 2, VLA, on RLinf piRL (pi0 or pi0.5, PPO with a critic):
- Task family: one ManiSkill pick-and-place family where the SFT policy completes the prefix (reach/grasp/lift) and the RL task adds the final placement or release, with binary success reward.
- Locator: train the done-probe on the action expert's pooled hidden state from the SFT demos (last 5 frames of each prefix segment vs earlier frames). Compute g per action chunk as d * (1 - V_hat).
- Noise: multiply the Flow-SDE or Flow-Noise noise scale by exp(beta * g), normalised to the batch mean so the total budget is unchanged; gripper dimension first.

designs.name: SoC (Split-on-Conflict): grow region-gated readout and exploration parameters where per-region PPO gradients oppose the rest
designs.one_line: After the first successes, detect latent regions of the reused representation whose PPO gradients on the shared readout or log-std persistently point against the rest of the state space, beyond a split-half noise null. Give only those regions a zero-initialised copy of the parameters, plus an exploration bonus at birth. This splits where PCGrad would project.
mechanism: 1. Reuse and protect as in SEAM: source actor init, frozen hidden layers. W, b (8x256 readout) and logsigma (8) are shared parameters. First successes come from any exploration source: in the pilot a global gripper boost, in the full method SEAM.

2. Regions in impression space. After iteration 1, run k-means (K=16, 20 Lloyd steps in torch) on h(s) = actor_mean[:-1](s) of the first rollout batch (51,200 states) and freeze the centroids; region r(s) is the nearest centroid. No labels and no target expert. Add zero-initialised region parameters dW_k (8x256), db_k (8), dlogsigma_k (8) and an 'active' mask. mu(s) = W h + b + active[r] * (dW_r h + db_r); logsigma(s) = logsigma + active[r] * dlogsigma_r. The function is unchanged when a region activates.

3. Conflict test, run after GAE and before the update (between ppo.py:479 and :497), on every iteration whose rollout has >= 10 successful episodes; before the first success it never runs. Use batch-normalised advantages A_i and per-sample score terms u_i = A_i (a_i - mu_i)/sigma_i^2 (mean) and v_i = A_i ((a_i - mu_i)^2/sigma_i^2 - 1) (log-std). For region k: G_k^W = mean over i in k of u_i h_i^T and G_k^sigma = mean over i in k of v_i; G_-k is the same over all other states. Region k is in conflict if either (a) cos(G_k^W, G_-k^W) < -0.1, or (b) on some action dimension, G_k^sigma and G_-k^sigma have opposite signs with |t| > 2 under within-region variance. The same part must also pass a split-half null: random halves of region k give cos > 0.3, or the same sign. The conflict must also hold in >= 3 of the last 5 tests. The null and persistence requirements exist because within-task sample conflicts can be as large as cross-task ones (Elich et al.).

4. Split, using the located conflict as an exploration signal. Activate at most one region per iteration and at most 4 of 16 in total. At birth set dlogsigma_k,d = +0.5 on dimensions whose region std-gradient is positive (deviating from the reused behaviour pays there), else 0, and dW_k = 0. Clamp dlogsigma to [-1, 1.5].

5. Learning. PPO updates W, b and logsigma from all samples. Active deltas receive gradient only from their region's samples, because they only enter mu and sigma there. A new action learned at a conflict region therefore cannot move the shared readout's behaviour elsewhere, and carry regions can shrink their own noise while the seam keeps its own.

6. Optional growth of impressions. With --soc_units m, a split also copies the m = 16 last-hidden-layer units most specific to region k (largest mean |activation| contrast) into trainable region-gated copies, with the originals frozen. This grows new features from old ones, only where conflict was measured; it is the user's 'grow new impressions'. Off in the pilot.

7. Logging for the mechanism claim: for each split, the iteration, the region, its phase composition from obs flags (grasped, |cube->goal| <= 2.5 cm, released near goal) and its learned std. This tests whether gradient conflict finds the seam without labels.
how_it_differs: PCGrad detects conflicts between task gradients and projects them at every step. SoC detects conflicts between state regions inside one task and resolves them structurally, by growing function-preserving region-gated copies. It also covers the exploration parameter (log-std), which PCGrad never touches.

Recon, GradPS, HarmoDT/SoCo-DT, CoNAL and the main agent's conflict_concentration.py all gate copies by task or agent and measure cross-task or cross-agent conflict (supervised, offline, MARL or BC). SoC gates by a region of the reused latent, measures conflict from the on-policy PPO score function within one task, uses a split-half null, and needs no target expert.

Soft Modularization, CMTA and MoE learn routing everywhere, end to end. SoC keeps everything shared until a significant, persistent conflict appears, then adds a zero-initialised copy for that region only.

Learned state-dependent noise (gSDE heads, TMRL, ReinFlow-style noise nets) adapts noise per state everywhere from the start; learned noise nets collapsed most tasks in Yardimci & Cogurcu 2026. SoC changes noise only in regions whose std-gradient opposes the rest, and adds an exploration bonus at birth.

Munos & Moore 1999 and U-Tree also split state cells where value or policy disagree, but in tabular or aggregation settings. SoC is that idea on top of frozen, reused deep features in on-policy deep RL, with function-preserving initialisation.

designs.name: CoSplit: split shared units where the RL loss pulls them in opposite directions
designs.one_line: Grow new impressions from old ones only where they conflict. During PPO, compute each hidden unit's splitting curvature (Liu et al. 2019) from the policy-gradient loss. Split a unit whose curvature falls well below a permuted-advantage null into two function-preserving children along the conflict direction. This is a structural, label-free, state-level alternative to PCGrad's projection. It is tested against random-split, fresh-growth and width-matched controls at equal parameter count.
mechanism: 1. Network. In Agent.actor_mean (wrwl/ppo.py:162-167), replace hidden layers 2 and 3 (Sequential indices 2 and 4) with GrowLinear(in, 256+R): R=64 reserve units and a buffer alive (1 for the first 256 units). The forward pass is a = tanh(Wx+b)*alive, and the next layer has 256+R input columns, of which the dead ones contribute 0. In every multi-task arm the critic gets one value head per task (selected by the task one-hot), and advantages are normalised per task over the whole batch, replacing the per-minibatch normalisation at ppo.py:511-512.

2. Statistics. Every 10 iterations from iteration 20, after the PPO update, take N=8192 rows of the current batch (b_obs, b_actions, normalised b_advantages). Forward the actor and keep, for each layer l in {2,3}: the layer input with a constant 1 appended (x~_l), the pre-activation z_l and the activation a_l. Compute logp = Normal(mu,sigma).log_prob(a).sum(1). G_l = autograd.grad(logp.sum(), a_l) gives each row's d log pi/d a_l, because a row's logp depends only on its own activations.

3. Splitting matrix (Liu et al. 2019, Def. 2.1, with sigma = tanh(w^T x~)). For the PPO surrogate at ratio 1, where clipping is inactive, the derivative of the loss with respect to the unit outputs is Phi'_l = -A*G_l/N. For unit j, S_j = sum_s Phi'_{l,j}(s) * tanh''(z_j(s)) * x~(s) x~(s)^T, where tanh''(z) = -2 tanh(z)(1 - tanh^2 z). Compute it for all alive units with one chunked einsum('sj,sa,sb->jab'). The null is the same computation with A randomly permuted across rows, which breaks the link between state and advantage but keeps the advantage distribution.

4. Detection. Keep EMAs S_bar <- 0.7 S_bar + 0.3 S, for the real statistic and for the null. A batched eigh gives each alive unit's splitting index lambda_j = lambda_min(S_bar_j) and splitting direction v_j. The layer threshold tau_l is the 1st percentile of that layer's null indices. A unit is conflicted when lambda_j < tau_l: different states pull its pre-activation in opposite directions along v_j, which one tanh unit cannot satisfy but two can. This is the second-order counterpart of GradPS's cancelled updates.

5. Split. Each split takes the k=8 most negative conflicted units per layer. The scheduled variant used for the matched comparison takes the 8 most negative units regardless of tau. Splitting stops when the R reserve units are used up. The reserve unit r gets [w_r, b_r] = [w_j, b_j] - eps*v_j, and the parent becomes [w_j, b_j] + eps*v_j. eps = 0.05/std_s(v_j^T x~(s)), so the two children's pre-activations differ by about ±0.05. In the next layer, set W'[:,r] = W'[:,j]/2 and W'[:,j] <- W'[:,j]/2. Set alive[r] = 1 and zero the Adam moments of the touched rows and columns. The policy is unchanged up to O(eps^2). Assert KL(new||old) < 1e-3 nats per decision on the batch, and halve eps if it is larger.

6. Training. The children then train as usual. Nothing else changes: same PPO loss, no extra loss term, and the split itself uses no task labels. Log the alive counts, lambda quantiles against the null, and each split's alignment |cos(v_j, xbar_task_k - xbar_others)|, to separate cross-task splits from within-task (phase) splits.

7. Controls, all at the same schedule and parameter count. Random-split: the unit is drawn uniformly among alive units, v is uniform on the sphere, and eps follows the same rule. Fresh-grow: the reserve unit gets orthogonal random input weights and a zero output column, so capacity grows without reusing the parent's impression. MT-wide: all 256+R units are alive from step 0.

8. Transfer use (S0 -> PushCubeDir theta=180). Load the source actor into the first 256 rows and columns, reset actor_logstd to -0.5, use a fresh critic, and start splitting at iteration 5. Source impressions that the target pulls in opposite directions are split; the rest stay shared and keep their function.
how_it_differs: vs PCGrad/CAGrad: these project or reweight conflicting gradients in parameter space and throw away part of each task's update. CoSplit keeps both updates by giving each side of the conflict its own copy of the unit, and a second-order test decides which units to split.

vs Recon (ICLR 2023) and GradPS (ICML 2025): those copy whole layers per task, or clone neurons per agent group, using first-order conflict scores and hard task or agent routing. CoSplit splits single units along the input direction of the conflict, at the state level and without task or agent labels. It therefore also resolves within-task phase conflicts (Elich et al. find these as large as cross-task ones), and the children are function-preserving.

vs Splitting Steepest Descent (NeurIPS 2019): there, splits grow compact supervised CNNs after convergence. Here the splitting index is computed from the PPO surrogate, with a permuted-advantage null and an EMA, and serves as a conflict detector during on-policy RL. It is checked against random-split and fresh-growth controls, which no RL paper we found reports.

vs Split-RL (NVIDIA, NeurIPS 2026): Split-RL sends locally conflicting updates into disjoint state regions inside gradient-boosted trees, using guidance labels. CoSplit does this inside a neural policy without labels, the mechanism Split-RL says neural networks lack.

vs our backup 'Aliased, Not Overloaded' and Gradient Coupling: both reshape the shared features with a separation loss on mined aliased pairs, labelled by advantage or by heuristics. That can distort shared impressions, and with sparse reward the labels are noise. CoSplit adds capacity and leaves the existing function unchanged at the moment of the split.

vs Memory Anchors: Memory Anchors locates conflict points to choose replay data, and its action-disagreement step needs new-task demonstrations. CoSplit changes the architecture and needs only the RL loss.

vs GPM / Adam-NSCL: projection protects old subspaces, but it cannot change aliased states whose activations lie inside the protected span. A split adds a direction v along which aliased states can be treated differently.

vs CARE / MOORE / Soft Modularization / MoE: these split capacity everywhere from the start, with learned routing conditioned on task or state. CoSplit starts dense and splits only the units where a conflict is detected.

pilot.setting:
A low-noise dense push family on our testbed. A new env, PushCubeMultiDir-v1, extends PushCubeDir-v1:
- theta in {0, 90, 180, 270} degrees is drawn per env at reset.
- The goal is visible, and a 4-d task one-hot is appended, giving a 39-d state.
- Cube spawn and robot are the same for all tasks, so it is a homogeneous same-scene suite (the state-based analogue of LIBERO-Goal, where Memory Anchors found conflicts concentrate).
- Reward is PushCubeDir's dense shaping, computed with each env's own direction.
- Panda pd_joint_delta_pos, 2048 envs x 20 steps, gamma 0.8 (as in M1), otherwise wrwl/ppo.py defaults.
- 10M env steps; deterministic eval on 256 envs every 5 iterations.

Transfer stage: S0 (runs/m1/runs/source_t0) -> PushCubeDir theta=180, dense, 5M steps. In M1, fine-tuning there took 2.6-3.4M steps to 80% against 0.9-1.3M from scratch, but M1's fine-tune arm also loaded S0's critic and log-std; this pilot separates those effects.

PushCube-v1 + PullCube-v1 through MultiTaskEnv (unified 78-d obs) can replace the new env, but that needs a multi-env PPO loop and steps the simulators one after another.
arms: Stage 0 (offline, ~0.1 GPU-h): splitting indices of S0's units under the theta=180 loss (MC returns minus a ridge baseline as advantages) against the same statistic under S0's own theta=0 loss and the permuted null
Stage 1 premise (3 seeds each): single-task scratch per theta (reuse M1's theta=0/90/180 runs; 3 new seeds at 270)
Stage 1: MT-plain, a shared actor and critic with batch advantage normalisation
Stage 1: MT-base, MT-plain plus per-task value heads and per-task advantage normalisation; its splitting diagnostics and cross-task actor/critic gradient cosines are logged
Stage 2 (only if the premise passes; all arms use per-task value heads and per-task advantage normalisation; 5 seeds): MT-base
Stage 2: MT-wide, a 3x320 actor from step 0 (the final parameter count of the grown arms)
Stage 2: MT-heads, a shared trunk with one actor readout per task (task-gated readout)
Stage 2: MT-PCGrad, with per-task actor gradients projected (3 seeds)
Stage 2: CoSplit, scheduled: 8 units per layer every 10 iterations from iteration 20, in hidden layers 2-3, up to +64 each
Stage 2: Random-split, same schedule and eps
Stage 2: Fresh-grow, same schedule, with new units that have random input weights and zero output weights
Stage 3 transfer (3 seeds): scratch; FT-fixed (S0 actor, fresh critic, log-std reset); frozen trunk + trainable readout; FT-fixed + CoSplit; FT-fixed + Random-split
pilot.metric:
Primary: deterministic eval success averaged over tasks, as AUC on [0, 10M] env steps. In Stage 3, AUC on [0, 5M] and T80.
Secondary: worst-task AUC, per-task T80 in per-task env steps, final success, parameter count.
Diagnostics: fraction of alive units whose splitting index is below the null's 1st percentile; cross-task cosine of per-task actor and critic gradients on shared layers; share of splits aligned with a task direction versus within-task.
pilot.success:
Premise (Stage 1) passes if both hold:
- MT-base per-task T80 is at least 1.3x the single-task T80, as a median over tasks and seeds.
- At least 5% of units fall below the null in at least half of the checks.

Method (Stage 2) succeeds if all hold:
- CoSplit beats Random-split, Fresh-grow and MT-wide on mean-task AUC by at least 0.05 each.
- The paired difference is positive in at least 4 of 5 seeds.
- CoSplit is not below MT-heads.

Transfer (Stage 3) succeeds if FT-fixed + CoSplit reaches T80 at no more than 0.8x min(scratch, FT-fixed) in 3 of 3 seeds.
pilot.kill:
Stop after Stage 1 if either holds:
- With the critic fixed, the shared network is less than 1.3x slower than single-task. Then the conflict is in the critic or nowhere, which is what MTBench found.
- Splitting indices never fall below the null.

Stop after Stage 2 if any holds:
- CoSplit minus Random-split is under 0.02 AUC, or its sign changes across seeds (which units are split does not matter).
- MT-wide or Fresh-grow is at least as good as CoSplit (capacity explains the gain).

Drop the transfer claim if FT-fixed + CoSplit is not faster than FT-fixed.

Stage 0 is an early warning only: if S0 shows no below-null curvature under the theta=180 loss, expect Stage 3 to fail.
